The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 91) to amend the Inland Waters Seamen's Act. He said : The existing Act defining the inland waters of Canada is very uncertain, and doubts have arisen as to what it really means. It says : ' All the waters of Canada above the city of Quebec.' The question was whether that was confined to the River St. Lawrence or whether it embraced the lakes, or whether it could embrace the waters of the great North-west Territories. I have brought in a Bill to define that the inland waters of Canada shall embrace all the rivers and lakes whose waters are navigable, excepting the sea-coasts, bays and harbours, from a line above Point des Monts and Cape Chat on the shores of the St. Lawrence ; and conferring upon the judge of the Supreme Court in the Yukon territory, and upon the judge of the territorial court in the North-west Territories, the same jurisdiction for the punishment of offences as is given to the judges of the Superior Court of Lower Canada, and to the judges of the 62+
sessions of the peace in the lower provinces, with regard to offences committed upon the high seas, within Canadian jurisdiction.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) moved for leave to introduce a Bill (No. 92) to amend the Act respecting the safety of ships. He said: When the Dominion Act was originally passed, many years ago, it then conformed to the British law. Since then the British mercantile law has been amended in very slight particulars, and owing to the construction of modern ships the spaces that are covered in and are not counted in the tonnage are not allowed by our law to be filled up with a cargo except by deals to the height of three feet, and I propose to amend our law so as to make it conform exactly with the Imperial statute in that respect.
Is that in respect to deck loads ?

I may say to my hon. friend that the Bill does not provide for any compulsory inspection of deck loads. It simply amends our existing law so as to provide that the vacant space, which is now compelled by law to be vacant, the spaces covered in in steamers above the three feet of deals, may be filled up with such articles as hay or other light material. It does not otherwise touch the question of deck loads at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time. .

The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) moved for leave to introduce a Bill (No. 93) respecting inquiries and investigations into shipping casualties. He said : The Bill is the result of many communications which have passed between the Board of Trade in England and the Marine Department in Canada. Under the law as it now stands, we have power to investigate into the causes of any casualty which occurs in Canadian waters, even if the ship is commanded by an officer holding a British certificate, a British officer. The officers holding British certificates complained that the manner in which our investigations were held did not ensure to them that perfect fair-play which is ensured to them by investigations held under the British system.
The Board of Trade, after several cases had taken place, and the evidence been

sent to them, intimated as their opinion that the investigation should partake more of a judicial character, and that the judge who heard the case and decided whether the officer should lose his certificate for carelessness, should have the advantage in all cases of competent nautical assessors to sit with him, and that the presiding judge should be a legal gentleman. The Bill has been drafted in accordance with the suggestions of the British Board of Trade, inasmuch as grave doubts exist, and there is a difference of opinion between the law officers of the Crown on this side of the water and the law officers of the Crown in Great Britain, as to whether the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had appellate jurisdiction to amend, or alter, or modify the findings of the court, the present law removes that doubt, and declares that he shall not have that jurisdiction ; so that, if a judicial court, under this statute, finds that an officer has been guilty of neglect of duty, the finding and the evidence are forwarded to Great Britain, to the authority from which he receives the certificate, to be dealt with by them, and cannot be altered or amended by us.
It is to British certificates that it relates ?

Entirely to British certificates. These are the two main amendments to enable me to appoint county court judges at Halifax, St. John and some other places and to associate with them nautical officers so as to bring our law into unison and harmony with the spirit of the British law and to make it uniform.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I understand the hon. gentleman proposes this change only in regard to certificates issued under the British Board of Trade in England ?
Precisely.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Our law as to men holding certificates issued by the Department of Marine here, remains as it is.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries retains the same power as he had before.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Yes, but in regard to the court of first instance, are the general legal requirements necessary to the hearing of this case the same ; for instance, supposing the hon. gentleman were to take Capt. Smith, or some other officer, and appoint him to hold a preliminary inquiry ?

Not necessarily to hold the Sir LOUIS DAVIES.
preliminary inquiry, but to hold an inquiry dealing with the certificate. We follow the same procedure as in England. The Bill provides for the appointment of a county judge, or a judge of some kind ta act. An assessor would proceed with the court and Capt. Smith could act as the assessor to the judge.

RICHARDSON (Lisgar) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 94) to amend the Railway Act. He said : Mr. Speaker, for the last two or three years the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) and myself have been endeavouring to get a clause inserted into charters in the Railway Committee, conferring upon His Majesty, or upon the government, power to expropriate a railway at any time that it is deemed in the public interest that such railway should be expropriated, and also providing that any bonuses which may be given to the railway may properly be deducted from the price agreed upon in regard to the expropriation of the road. Upon every occasion upon which we have endeavoured to get that clause inserted in a charter in the Railway Committee, we were met by the proposition that it is singling a particular railway out for special treatment, and that there would be no objection if a clause of this kind were made to apply generally. I thought it would be in the interest of the House and the country that a Bill of that nature should be brought before the House.
I have brought it in as an amendment to the Railway Act, and it contains only three provisions. One of the provisions, as I have explained, is that when you take over the road, any subsidies which have been voted to it shall be deducted. I have added to that provision that this clause shall apply to charters granted from the date of the existence of the present parliament. I may say that I looked up the question of the expropriation of railways, and I find that in 1884, Mr. Gladstone introduced a Bill into the Imperial House of Commons which became law, providing conditions under which railways might be expropriated by the government. After thinking the matter over, to some extent, I decided that it would not be well to insert in the Bill any provision ^ of that nature, but that I should simply ask ' the House to make a general declaration in favour of expropriation. I regret that I was not in possession of certain information when we last had the matter before the Railway Committee, because, I find that we are not establishing a precedent at ail. The first Canadian railway charter that was ever granted to a company, the proprietors of the Champlain and St. Lawrence Railroad, provided that the government should have the

right to expropriate the road at any time upon paying to the proprietors the amounts paid on their shares, plus 20 per cent. The Act incorporating the Grand Trunk Railway Company provided that the government might purchase the railway at the end of twenty-one years from January 1,1853, upon certain conditions. The Act incorporating the London and Gore Railway Company, which in 1845 became the Great Western, provided for expropriation by the government at any time after forty years after completion of the work, upon repayment of the amounts paid on shares, plus 20 per cent. In many other charters there is an expropriation clause, so that I am not asking the House to establish any precedent whatever. I think It is desirable that this power should be made general. I am quite prepared for the argument that parliament has control of the railways now, but I think it is as well that we should serve formal notice upon all railway companies from this time forth, that their property may be expropriated by the Dominion, if necessary. Then, there will be no obtaining money from capitalists in the old land under false pretenses. They will clearly understand that a provision exists under which parliament may take these roads over. I think, in view of the trend of public opinion in favour of government control, or government ownership of railways, that it is particularly desirable that the Bill of which I have given notice shall be adopted. I move for leave to introduce the Bill, seconded by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson).
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

I desire to move the addition of another clause to the Bill, in accordance with the terms of the notice which I gave a few days ago. I move that the following be added as clause 14 :
His Majesty shall have the right at any time to take over the undertaking, property, rights and franchises of the company, and for that purpose the provisions of the Expropriation Act shall apply.
From any valuation placed upon such property so taken there shall be deducted on payment the amount of any bonus or subsidy paid by the government of Canada to the company towards the construction of such line of railway or any part thereof.
This resolution is somewhat similar in terms to a resolution which was presented to the committee and the House when a Bill similar to this was under our consideration some twelve months ago. If this were a Bill asking for an ordinary local charter, for the construction of a road seventy-five miles long for the purpose of serving the municipalities through which it passed, there might be some valid objection taken to the insertion of this provision. But the charter asked for is not for the purpose of constructing a local road ; that has never been sought for, and it is not required. Between the town of Collingwood, one of the termini mentioned in the Bill, and Lake Ontario we have already two roads-one running to the city of Toronto, ninety-four miles in length, and the other running to the city of Hamilton, about 112 miles in length. So that the two chief ports on Lake Ontario are connected with that important port on the Georgian Bay by two lines of railway whose greatest distance apart is not more than twenty-five miles. It cannot be said, therefore, that this third road is required for any purposes of a local character. That, I think,
has been made abundantly clear again and again in debates which have taken place in this House on the transportation question, and by representations which have been made by the leading business men and organizations of the province of Ontario ; and if the committee and the House had not been impressed with the view that the road which we propose to charter was to form a link in a transportation route the most direct between the head of inland navigation and the sea-board, I think great difficulty would have been experienced in procuring a charter for the construction of this road. It is proposed that this shall be made an air line. The distance from Collingwood to Toronto by the present rail route is ninety-four miles. By constructing this line in the most direct way, it is expected that the distance will be shortened to seventy or seventy-four miles. Large bonding powers have been given in the Bill, because it is proposed that the road shall be constructed in the most substantial manner possible, with the heaviest rails, the most substantial road-bed, the latest and most improved freight cars, and the heaviest and best locomotives, for the purpose of carrying on the large business which we all hope and expect will be developed between the west and north-west and the sea-board in years to come. The board of trade of the city of Toronto for some years past, being impressed with the importance of this route as a competitive route against the railways, has been drawing public attention to the matter, and has been invoking the aid of the government for the purpose of securing the construction of a line similar to that which is proposed under this Bill ; and I have in my hand a copy of a resolution which was adopted unanimously at a general meeting of that board, held on the 2nd of February, 1899, and Which declared :
That, in the opinion of this board, the Dominion government should take into consideration the question of opening up this most important avenue of communication with the seaboard, and that, in connection with the canal system of this country, they should complete the shortest and most speedy route to the upper lakes by building an independent railway to operate in connection with vessels from Toronto, which is the most suitable harbour on Lake Ontario, and the nearest and most suitable harbour or harbours for the purpose upon the Georgian Bay, as a complement to the St. Lawrence canal system.
On June 1, 1899, the Toronto Board of Trade adopted unanimously the recommendation respecting the means to be adopted to create more Canadian bottoms on our lakes. Among the means which could best accomplish this object was the construction of
A line of railway to be owned and controlled by the government, built across the portage to Georgian Bay, which is the natural receptacle of the grain of the United States as well as of western Canada, the ports of which are able to accommodate the largest vessels which traverse the upper lakes, but which cannot get in to Lake Ontario, thus making a short and speedy route to Chicago, Duluth and Fort William, with opportunities for return cargo, especially of manufactured products for the Canadian North-west. By this project centres of population, including points as far east ias the maritime provinces, Quebec, Montreal and Toronto, become interested in a common aim to build up our lake marine and create an interprovincial marine trade.
I draw attention to these conclusions of the Toronto Board of Trade to emphasize the point, that in all the discussions which have taken place so far, this line of railway was not considered as a local enterprise but as .merely a link, and a comparatively short link in the chain of communication between the head of Lake Superior and the city of Quebec.
When the matter was up for consideration twelve months ago, the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy), who was deeply interested in this subject, made some remarks on the transportation question, introduced by the resolution of my hon. friend the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett), and in the course of remarks made on the 28th March last, the hon. member for North Simcoe said :
If this railway were built, the chain would be complete, and thus the natural channel through which this trade should go would be perfected, and the lower lakes, rivers and canals would be successfully joined with the upper lakes and canals.
The hon. member then went on to give statements showing the distances by the various routes now adopted between the head of Lake Superior and the ports of Montreal and Quebec, but I need not weary the committee by giving these tables of distances, as they can be found in the 'Hansard' of March 28th last. He concluded by making the statement that ' there seems to be no room for doubt that the route via Collingwood and Toronto is of all the cheapest and best.' But this route of course cannot be made available except by the construction of this air line for the purpose of joining together the ports of Collingwood and Toronto.
Now. the hon. member who represented Kent in the last parliament (Mr. Campbell), who is one of the promoters of this Bill, joined in that discussion twelve months ago and had something to say as to the advantages which he thought would result, not only to the producers of the west and the North-west, but also to the people of the province of Ontario, if this railway were constructed and this route established. Speaking on the same day as the hon. member for North Simcoe, the 28th March last, Mr. Campbell said :
I am strongly of opinion that the great highway from the west should be by way of the

It differs from the clause submitted last year in this respect, that it proposes to take over the entire enterprise, not the railway and appurtenances alone, hut the railway and whatever vessels are connected with it in the navigation of the great lakes. It is surely not unreasonable to ask that if the government of the day gives a substantial bonus to assist in the construction of this railway, the amount of the bonus should be deducted from the amount payable by the government, should it decide to take over the road.
I therefore beg to move that the following clause be added to the Bill :
His Majesty shall have the right at any time to take over the undertaking, property rights and franchises of the company, and for that purpose the provisions of the Expropriation Act shall apply.
From any valuation placed upon such property so taken there shall be deducted on payment the amount of any bonus or subsidy paid by the government of Canada to the company towards the construction of such line of railway or any part thereof.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
The question involved in the motion of the hon. gentleman was thoroughly threshed out before the Railway Committee, and I need not say that there was considerable diversity of opinion, first, as to whether the clause of this character at all should be introduced, and next, as to what its nature should be.
In the course of that discussion I expressed a certain view and framed an amendment embodying that view, and that amendment, which I proposed to the committee, is identical with that which the hon. gentleman has just moved. But it did not meet with the approval of the committee, and hence the hon. gentleman has felt it necessary to move it here. The question that is before the committee, it seems to me, is not a very large question, viewed from the standpoint of the promoters, nor is it one which, so far as I am capable of forming an opinion on the subject, ought in the slightest degree to militate against the promotion of the undertaking. I cannot conceive why any one who is satisfied that this enterprise had merit in it which would justify him in investing his means in it should hesitate to do so because this clause, if adopted by the committee, was found in the Bill. The first portion of the clause is little more than a declaration or notice that parliament may do, in respect of this particular undertaking what, unquestionably, it can do, without incorporating the clause in the incorporating Bill, in respect of any undertaking that may be set on foot through our legislation. Parliament, undoubtedly, as I view the law and the powers of parliament, can declare in favour of the expropriation of any property that it is deemed necessary in the public interest to possess, even though the company

which may have constructed that work and may have received its charter from this parliament did not take its charter with any express provision to that effect contained in it. The committee thought, or a number of the members of the committee thought, it would be desirable to give the notice, and I could see no objection to such notice being given, because it would simply convey to the promoters and to those investors who might connect themselves with the enterprise that this parliament has this power, which, otherwise, they might not be aware of. I do not consider that portion of the clause the important portion, but rather the second portion of it. This second part, as hon. members will see, provides that, in the event of parliament expropriating, the amount paid shall be subject to reduction by the amount of any subsidy or aid which may be given by this parliament to assist the enterprise. Now, it seems to me that practically the sole question for this committee to consider is whether or not it would be a reasonable or appropriate clause to insert in the Bill or a proper condition to impose. Will any person hesitate to say that it would be a proper condition ? I question if there is a doubt in the mind of any one in this House that, if we grant a subsidy to this road, and if the enterprise is of the importance which hon. gentleman, on both sides apparently, declare it to be-though I have not seen much evidence to convince me of that, but assuming that to be the case-and for that reason it was decided to acquire it, it would be proper to deduct from the value paid for the undertaking the amount of any subsidy granted by this parliament. I am prepared, for one, and so declared myself in this committee, to vote for this amendment. I think it can do no harm to anybody. I cannot see why any one should think it ought to militate at all against the succeseful promotion of the enterprise. What reason could any person have for refusing to go into this enterprise under such conditions ? If they were going in merely for the purpose of getting the bonus as a benefit to be retained by them even though the property were expropriated, I can imagine they would hesitate. But we will not assume that that motive would inspire anybody who would put his money into the undertaking. These are my views as expressed in the committee and as still entertained, and I am prepared to vote for the amendment the hon. gentleman has moved.

I take the liberty of asking the attention of . the Minister of Railways to an amendment to the amendment which I shall move. It is not necessary that we should here enter into a discussion of the merits or demerits of this road. But, if the government purposes taking over this road or any road to the Georgian Bay, I would respectfully submit
that a road leading to the harbour of Midland, which is a much better harbour than that of Collingwood, and which would not require the expenditure of any public money upon it in order to fit it to receive the largest vessels, would be much preferable to one to Collingwood. Still further, if the government is ever going to take over this road, by running to Midland and on to Parry Sound, there would be the beginning of a great national system of railways to the North-west which has been mentioned by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). The government would have at its disposal, from Toronto to Parry Sound, a road in full running order, which would save the construction of another road in case the one to Collingwood was built. As regards these two amendments, I am glad to hear the Minister of Railways and Canals say he will accept that one proposed by the member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). It was discussed in committee, and I believe that while it was voted down there, if we had had the support of the Minister of Railways

at the second reading we would have got it through. I hope under any case it will be put through to-day. In connection with the remarks made here to-day by the Minister of Railways, and already made before the committee, I wish to inform the House, and to inform his colleague, the Minister of Public Works, that somehow the minister does not think much of this proposition. Then, why is all this money being spent on Collingwood harbour ? Surely that harbour is to be improved at the public expense for a definite purpose, and If it is not in connection with a railway complementary of the canal system of this country, for what purpose is the money being spent ? I cannot see. Now, I suppose this road, or a similar road, is an important link in the railway and water transportation of this country. I am surprised to hear the minister say, as he has said on two occasions, that he does not think much of this proposition. While I will vote for the amendment, I must take the opportunity to say that I think the government is making a great mistake in allowing this charter to be taken up by a private corporation. As I argued in the Railway Committee, and as I will argue now, the government should expropriate the Grand Trunk Railway between Toronto and Collingwood, and nationalize a road between Toronto and some harbour on the Georgian Bay-Midland, probably, or Collingwood. But, certainly they could find a harbour, and then they could take over the better portion of the Grand Trunk Railway, double track it. and extend it on to Parry Sound and Sudbury, by North Bay on to Hudson Bay, in connection with the system of the Ontario government. But here is a proposition to get this road, which is the best paying road in Canada, and it could be acquired for what will be given in the way of bonuses to this country. If the government would pursue the policy they have declared of doing great things in connection with the canals of this country, they would not rest a moment until they did have a national railway from the Georgian Bay to Lake Ontario, and connecting with the railway and river system of this country. I am surprised mat this opportunity is to be let pass, as many others have been, without the government getting a substantial advantage to the country. As regards the proposal of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes), I think it is objectionable to interfei'e on behalf of municipalities. I think municipalities ought to make their own contracts when they vote their own money to railways.

speechtext: I am sorry my hon. friend from Essex (Mr. Cowan) is not here to discuss this Bill, as he is in charge of it; but, unfortunately, he is not able to do so to-day. speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Such being the case, why should wb single out this railway when you are making a general Act ? I am in favour of making a general Act dealing with all railways alike, and I think it is unfair to the promoters of this Bill. This Bill passed this House last year, it has passed the committee this year, we have already voted down a resolution proposed by the minister to-day, and I think it will be most unfair to the promoters of this Bill to have anything of that kind placed in it. maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to define my position upon this Bill and I will do it as briefly as possible. I do not propose to commence voting for legislation not according to my understanding of the lines we have been pursuing in the Railway Committee and in the House in times past. I believe that either one of these amendments will be a departure from the well-understood principles that we have hitherto followed. This is simply, as I understand it, a private Bill for a private railway.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. According to my understanding it is. It has been introduced and passed so far entirely as a private Bill. I think I am quite right and I propose to try to be logical. If, at any future time the government see fit, whichever party may be in power, and it becomes a public matter to adopt the policy which has been proposed, they must stand or fall upon that policy. In the general Railway Act last year, or the year before, wo had quite extensive alterations when the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair) revised it and put in a number of new clauses that wore in line with the policy of the government. If the government at the commencement of the session had made the announcement that they proposed to amend the Railway Act in this direction and apply the amendment to all the Bills that should be passed, there would be more logic in the proposition. I have always endeavoured, and I do not propose to change now, to legislate on legislative principles without departing from those in any special case. I say that the Railway Committee, haying passed this Bill, which was introduced as a private Bill, I propose to vote against both of these amendments. I propose to vote against the amendment of the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) because municipalities, if they give bonuses to this road, ought to be allowed to give them on such conditions as they please, as we have no jurisdiction over them. We are asked to say that a municipality cannot give a bonus in spite of this. If we pass the amendment to the amendment, it will be equivalent to our saying that we will take it out of the power of the municipality to give a bonus without any reference to getting it back at all. I think the municipal councils are quite competent to take care

197G
of themselves, and that they will not thank us for trying to tie their hands before the event or before they come to consider the question of the bonus. As to the amendment, if it is proposed to change the general Railway Act and apply expropriation, we can then consider the question, but I do not propose, as far as I am concerned, to vote to put this condition in any one particular Bill. I will say, in passing, now, though perhaps it might be more properly said afterwards, that I do not think this railway is entitled to a subsidy from the government, but that is a matter that we must deal with at the proper time. We neither should assume that it will get a bonus, or not get one, because that is a matter upon which the government will taae the responsibility at the proper time. Assuming that something is going to happen that we do not know will happen is something that we have no right to do in considering legislation of this kind. I have never legislated nor agreed to legislate in that way, and I do not propose to commence to-day. We can consider the question of the application of the expropriation power to Bills of this kind at the proper time. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) has introduced a Bill under which this question may be discussed. This Bill is nothing more nor less than a private Bill. Objections may be taken to the charter if any lion, gentleman wants to object to it, such as that the road is not necessary because it is paralleling an existing road, but, so far, we have never applied that principle and there is no objection to this Bill on that score.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: If this had been an ordinary private Bill granting permission to construct a road 70 miles long from one point to another in a territory already served by two railways, would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tisdale) vote for the charter ?

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: As a rule, I will vote for a railway charter where the promoters ask for no public aid, but where they will undertake to construct the road as a commercial undertaking, unless it is interfering with some road under construction.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: There are two lines under construction.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Suppose there are three. The only circumstances upon which we object to a charter are when there is [DOT]one road authorized already that is under construction and the time is not up. My view is that wo should legislate on legislative principles. If we do not we become personal. If we become personal, or party, in regard to private legislation, then, God help this House. The only logical and consistent way is to treat all individuals under similar circumstances alike. That I have endeavoured to do in the past and I propose to do in the future.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose that ordinarily I ought to oppose the Bill altogether, because it seems to me that there is only one point where grain ought to be transhipped to be sent down the St. Lawrence. However, I do not take so narrow a view as that in discussing the Bill which is now before the House. I am not opposing the Bill, but I am opposed to both of these amendments that have been presented to the House. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair) has said that the first part of the amendment is not at all necessary, because parliament has at all times the right to expropriate undertakings of this kind. Then, there only remains the question of the latter part of the amendment. I am speaking of the amendment of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), and that is providing that upon expropriation the amount of the subsidy is to be deducted. This amendment provides for the expropriation by the government of the whole undertaking. I do not want to put it in the power of the government to make an expropriation such as this amendement contemplates. If parliament has such power, or ever should choose to exercise that power, it will be a matter which should receive the most careful consideration of the House . If any one should propose the expropriation of the vessels, such as the hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Calvert) spoke of, as being the intention of this company to build for service on the upper lakes and to carry grain to Montreal, I think that will be a new departure, so far as government works are concerned, that will hardly meet the approbation of the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean). At least I hardly think so. It will be going a great deal farther than mere nationalizing the railway system of this country. I hope the government will not enter into competition with the private owners of vessel property by seeking to carry grain from the west to the east. I think this can be better done by private enterprise than by the government. Whatever may be said in reference to railways, telegraph lines, the telephone system, and similar enterprises, I do not think the argument applies to the government ownership of vessel property. Then, there is another thing. It strikes me as one of the strongest possible arguments that it is unfair discrimination against this company that such a clause should be put into their Bill. This is unquestionably a private Bill in reference to a company just such as we are incorporating all the time, and the logic of such an argument is irresistible. In view of the legislation which has heretofore been adopted by this House, I do not see what good reason can be given for incorporating in this Bill a clause which has not been incorporated in any other Bill in the past, and which it is not proposed to incorporate in any Bill in the future.
