maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: This railway is declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, and I am inclined to agree with the view of the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) that in respect to such works it would be desirable to pass a general law enabling the government of Canada to expropriate them.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: That is a different question.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not think it is a different question, and for this reason. You must begin at some time or other with a provision of this kind and there would be exactly the same reason against a general law that there is against this. If we are to start with the assumption that from henceforth the amendment wmcn is proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) shall be applied to all railways, then we must adopt that principle if we insert the clause in this Bill. I do not see any injustice in beginning with this company any more than beginning with any other company. I do not see any more injustice in doing this (provided we make it a principle which shall guide us in the future) than there would be injustice in passing a general Act; because any company coming after the general Act had been passed would be in the same position as this company and as all future companies under the principle I have indicated. I do not however agree with the terms of the amendment, and I do not agree with the views of the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) with regard to the justice of this amendment. The latter part of the amendment is expressed in this way :
From any valuation placed upon the said property so taken shall be deducted in payment the amount of any bonus or subsidy by the government of Canada to the company towards the construction of any such line of railway or any part thereof.
The objection I have to the amendment, and the objection I have to the argument of the
minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) is this : that while it might be in some cases perfectly proper to deduct the subsidy, it does not seem to me that in all cases it would be proper to do so. This amendment refers to the Expropriation Act. We all know the basis on which you work out the value of an undertaking under the Expropriation Act. You do not work it out on the basis of what it cost the persons who have constructed the undertaking; you work it out upon the basis of what the property is worth at the time of its expropriation. The rule in England, and I think in this country, is to add about 10 per cent to that for the reason that the property is taken against the will of the owner. Suppose this property at the time it is to be expropriated should be worth only half of what it had cost to the persons who had constructed it ; it does not seem to me that it would be a just thing to deduct the amount of the subsidy in a case of that kind. On the other hand if the property should be worth immensely more than it cost to construct it, it might be a very proper thing indeed, that the government in taking this road back should deduct the amount of the subsidy. The question came up incidentally in the discussion in respect to the value of the Drummond County Railway. That was not a case of expropriation, but it was a case in which the government were taking over a railway at a fixed price. The view I expressed then and to which I still adhere, is that if you take into consideration as a basis of your purchase the actual cost to the owner, then it is a most proper thing that you should deduct the subsidy after allowing interest or a reasonable advance to the person whose property you are taking. I took the view then, and I take it now that if you are dealing simply with the value of the property it does not seem to me that it would be in all cases a proper thing to deduct the amount of the subsidy, and indeed in some cases if you do so it might work a very great injustice to the owners of the road. For that reason I would not feel inclined to agree with the latter portion of the amendment, while I am in accord with the views expressed by the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair), and by the hon. member (Mr. Clarke) with regard to the first part of it. It may be there is some fallacy in the view I have expressed with regard to expropriation proceedings, and I should be glad if my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Blair) would point out any error in that respect.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman from Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) objects to this clause because this is a private Bill, and because we have not done this heretofore. His reasons do not hold good in my opinion. We can never commence too soon to do a right thing and it is never too late to mend a bad principle. If we believe that this is a proper thing to do,

19S0
then the fact that we have no precedent for it should not deter us. England has been carrying out the same principle for years. It is provided in England that every large vessel which is built according to the Admiralty requirements and which gets governmental subsidies shall be available to be taken over by the government at a certain valuation to be agreed upon in case of war. In this case we provided that this railway shall be taken over in the event of some important national necessity, and as we propose to give a subsidy in this case-

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: No, we do not.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: If there is no subsidy given to this road, then the clause does not apply at all.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: It does not have to apply. No harm is done.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: This proposed amendment certainly presumes that we will give a subsidy.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Not necessarily.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: It certainly does or else there is no sense in the amendment. Of course the first part of the clause declares our right to expropriate, and the Minister of Railways tells us that we have that right already, but the second part says we shall deduct the subsidy if we take over the road, and how can we deduct the subsidy if none is given. I repeat that the principle embodied in this amendment has been in force in England for half a century or more, in connection with the taking over of merchant vessels in case of war. These vessels are owned and built by private corporations and there is no difference between attacking a private corporation for the national need in England and attacking private corporation in case of national necessity here. The argument of the hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) consequently does not hold good. I am not in favour of the amendment to the amendment which proposes to deduct municipal bonuses. A municipality in giving a bonus gives it for the purpose of securing a railway for carrying trade to and from the locality, and when the railway is built the local need for which it pays the subsidy is satisfied and is never taken, away. It is only given by the people in the locality, who can always use this local convenience, and the cost of which is partly supplied by themselves. In that event I do not think there are just grounds why the municipality should ask for the money to be paid back. In addition to that, when a municipality gives a bonus, it costs nearly half of it to get the bonus carried ; and thus a large part of it is practically lost and does not inure to the advantage of the railway. But in this case, every person in the country contributes a portion of the cost

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: of the railway, both those who use the railway and those who do not. Therefore, when there is a national need that the railway should be taken under the control of the government, I can see no reason why the amount of the purchase price should not be reduced by the amount of the bonus given. The only reason is that stated by the leader of the opposition, which I confess has always been to my mind an argument against this principle. It was this. Suppose we give a subsidy to a private corporation, which goes on and builds the railway, and afterwards transfers it to innocent purchasers. The road runs down in the meantime until it becomes worth less than the original subsidy ; so that if the government took it at a valuation, and deducted the amount of the subsidy, the innocent holder would have nothing. It seems to me that the proposal of the hon. leader of the opposition is a very good one for safeguarding the interests of the innocent holders-that the subsidy should be deducted only when the value of the property exceeds the actual cost. That could. only be when it would become a matter of national importance that the government should take the railway under its control. The hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) says this is only a private corporation. There is no doubt that it is, and yet nobody would have given a charter to a private corporation to compete with others occupying the same ground, but for the national need. There are two private corporations occupying the same ground to-day ; and yet we are giving this company this charter because this road is believed to be a part of a great highway of commerce that will be of national importance, not only to Canada but to the United States as well ; because it is hoped it will attract a large part of the commerce of the United States. This road will serve not only the port of Collingwood, but any other ports on the Georgian Bay. At the present time there is a very important harbour being constructed at Meaford, and it has a sufficient depth of water to admit the largest vessels. Then, they have built a large elevator there for the purpose of securing a share of the trade of the upper lakes. Collingwood is only twenty-two miles from Meaford, and the road between the two places is almost as level as a floor. If this road becomes the national highway which we think it is destined to become, Meaford will be able to take advantage of it as well as Collingwood. It becomes the more important on that account, because it will be fed not simply by one good harbour, but by two. I think we should provide that when it becomes necessary in the interest of the country to take the road over, the government should not be obliged to pay the money which the country has put in to help to build it. That would be paying the money twice. For these reasons I am in favour of the amendment.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: I regret that I cannot agree with the last speaker in favouring this amendment. I opposed it in the Railway Committee, and I intend to oppose it here, for two reasons : first of all, for the reason which has been very lucidly stated by the hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale), that this is exceptional legislation, and if it is a sound principle to adopt, it should be adopted in a general way. I do not think it is a sufficient answer to say that we must make a beginning, and that we might as well begin here as anywhere else. We might begin to-day by applying the principle to this Bill, and to-morrow we might discuss the matter more thoroughly and come to the conclusion that it is, as I hold it to be, an unsound principle. So that one day we would have a Bill with this provision, and the next day we would have one in which it was not contained.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the hon. gentleman supported this principle in the Bill of last year ?

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: I have no recollection of having supported any such proposition, and if I did, that is no reason why I should support it now. On the contrary, I am always open to conviction. Supposing the proposition to deduct subsidies were proposed in a general Bill, there would be a great deal to be said on both sides of the question; the argument does not all lie on the one side. The point is this. When the government conclude to give a bonus for the construction of a railway, why do they do so? They do it in general, I believe, because they know that the dividends likely to arise from operation of the railway will not be sufficient to induce private capital to invest in the enterprise. In other words, the capital put in, tegether with the bonus, does not create a property as valuable as the bonus and the capital combined, and perhaps only creates one worth as much as the private capital put into it. I have in my mind a railway in the province of Nova Scotia into which the Dominion and provincial governments put subsidies amounting to about $500,000, and private capitalists put nearly $1,000,000, and they created a property which, if the government desired to take it over, would probably have been valued at less than $1,000,-000-perhaps at $600,000 or $700,000. The result of such a provision in that case would be that private individuals would be asked to construct a property for the benefit of the whole country, and lose $400,000 or $500,000 of their own money in the effort to do so. I do not believe that Is a right or equitable result, and I do not believe that the proposition applied as a general principle would be likely to operate as the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) supposes that it would. Instead of being any relief to the poor people who are sweating and groaning under the fardels which they have to bear in this matter of railway construction, it might increase their burdens, by making it more difficult to construct railways in this country. It is perhaps not necessary to go into the discussion of that subject at present; but I say it is not a sound principle, capable of application in every case, to deduct the bonus from the value of the property. It would be confiscating the property, and compelling private individuals to construct railways for the benefit of the country at large. In this particular case, it is absolutely indefensible, because it is proposed to make it an exception, instead of introducing the principle as a general one applicable to every one alike.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Is not the hon. gentleman at the present time advocating the taking over by the government of a provincial railway in Nova Scotia, and giving back to the province the bonuses given to it by the provincial government ? It is the same principle.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: When did I advocate that?

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
If we could get from the right hon. leader of the House a declaration as to whether he would be willing to accept, as a government measure, the Bill which I introduced this afternoon, and which, I gather from the remarks of the Minister of Railways, would have that hon. gentleman's support, this discussion might end here. The Bill I have introduced merely provides for the expropriation of any railway, when parliament decides that its expropriation is in the interests of the country, and provides further for the deduction of the government bonuses from the expropriation, price, as proposed by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke).
I want to say a word with reference to the contention of the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) and the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell), that we would, if we should adopt this amendment, be creating a precedent. Hon, gentlemen will remember how frequently that argument was used in the last two or three sessions.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: I did not use the argument that you would be using any precedent. I am of the opinion that we would not and that it would not be observed as a precedent.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman did not use that argument, but the argument was generally used that it would be unfair

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not agree with the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I have no desire to misrepresent any one, but it was generally contended that it would be unfair to single out any particular company for the application of this provision, and that the proper way was to bring this up in the House of Commons as a general Act. I

have a good deal of sympathy with that view, and it was in order to get a declaration from the House on the general principle that I introduced the Bill I did this afternoon. There may be some provisions in that Bill which the House may not think desirable, and I would be prepared to accept any amendment that would render it more workable.
With regard to the establishment of a precedent, this would not have the effect, because a precedent has already been established. In 1844, in the parliament of Great Britain, Mr. Gladstone introduced an Act, which is now in the statutes, containing just such a provision as the one proposed, namely, that at any time parliament may expropriate any railway.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: I did not argue for one moment that we could not pass a general law, and the hon. gentleman is misrepresenting me.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am not making the slightest reference to the hon. gentleman at all. My observations are purely of a general character. I am saying that in 1844 a precedent was established in the British parliament. Also in the first railway charter which ever passed the parliament of Canada the Act incorporating the proprietors of the Champlain and St. Lawrence Railway, there is a provision for government expropriation at any time, on paying to the proprietors the amount paid on their shares, plus 20 per cent. In the charter of the Grand Trunk Railway there is also a clause providing for expropriation, so that if the government desired to take over the Grand Trunk Railway, from Collingwood down, we have the power to do so under the charter of that company itself. Then, in the Act incorporating the Great Western Company, originally known as the London and Gore Railway Company, there is just such a clause providing for expropriation. And if hon. gentlemen choose to look through the statutes, they will find many railway charters giving this power of expropriation.
We are asked, why single out this company to begin with ? Well, there is no desire on the part of any one to single out this particular company. It is promoted by a gentleman who has always been deservedly popular in this House and generally respected, and it is particularly painful to me to have to offer any opposition at all, because of my desire to agree with and ass'st that hon. gentleman. But we have to begin somewhere, and is not the present just as good a time as any other ?
I agree with the Minister of Railways that if this parliament, or any municipality or province, contributes to a railway enterprise, and the people desire to take that road over for its own benefit, the subsidy paid should be deducted from the price awarded. Why should we hand over the subsidy itself ? In Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
giving a company the privilege to build a railway, we confer a valuable franchise, and if in addition we give a bonus, why should the people not be returned that bonus when taking over the railway.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: The government have not given bonuses to this road, and have ample power to expropriate any time they think fit. The hon. gentleman wants to expropriate before any bonuses are granted.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways explained that point fully in the committee. He showed that there was no power in the general Railway Act, or even in the Expropriation Act, to deduct the government bonus. Parliament, of course, can exercise the right of eminent domain and expropriate anything, but we want to serve notice on all companies from this time out.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: I did not say that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Well, some one used that argument. I repeat that it would be.desirable we should serve notice that from this time forth parliament may expropriate any railway it may deem in the interests of Canada to take over. Then the men who put money into these enterprises will know that such a provision exists. They may not stop to think that parliament is supreme, and may exercise its right of eminent domain, but when put in a general Bill, such as the one I propose, they cannot plead ignorance. Unless, however, we have the promise that the Bill I propose will pass this session, we ought to insist on the clause suggested being put into this particular measure.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I have not heard any reason advanced why this should be made an exceptional case. Of course, the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) said that this was not an ordinary road, but I do not think that any member of this House will admit that there is anything in that statement. During the past few years we have granted a great many charters very much more extraordinary, and they met with no particular opposition. What I want to point out is that some years ago, in order that we might have unanimity with regard to Bills of this kind, a committee was appointed, and a model Bill was adopted, and this measure is strictly along the lines of that model Bill.	We have given
charters in the past with very much wider and more extraordinary powers. But, for the sake of having uniformity, the most experienceed men in these matters got together and framed a model Bill; and that model Bill has been pretty closely stuck to, except in cases where some good reason was shown for variation. In this case, I am safe in saying, no reason at. all has
been given. My bon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) says that this is an important railway, and that the Toronto Board of Trade has had the subject before it. I will admit that the members of the board of trade have been squabbling about this road for a great many years. But, we have not found these members of the board of trade, nor. the citizens of Toronto, coming forward to put a dollar into this enterprise. If it is such an important and extraordinary enterprise, if it is going to do such a tremendous trade, it is strange that these men who are investing money and raising money in other countries for railway enterprises, have not found it of advantage to themselves or the country to make or promote investment in it. The fact is, we had a little local squabble in Toronto. But we have had before the committee, Bill after Bill of a hundred times as much importance as this, we have had such Bills go through every session, and not a word along the lines of the proposed amendment. I can only come to one conclusion-that there is thought to be a special effort now to move a seductive looking amendment. I am prepared to say that there may not be something in the principle or policy involved in the amendment ; but, I think that no one who seriously desired the future prosperity of tile country would be able to announce off-hand whether he favoured the principle of that amendment or not. As has been ably pointed out by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Bussell), it is a question whether this, instead of being a movement in the public interest, if seriously and closely examined, may not be found" to involve a most mistaken policy. I believe that what we want in this country is the development of our resources ; we want people with capital, whether Canadians or outsiders, to invest in railway enterprises under proper conditions. We have had a great deal of experience in these matters, and, as a result of that experience, we adopted a model Bill. Subject to the conditions that our experience has shown to be necessary, we should give every encouragement we can to railway enterprises. If the time ever comes, after we have granted a charter in the ordinary manner, when the parties who have the charter appeal for a subsidy, or bonus or assistance, then is the time l'or any hon. member to declare on what conditions it is thought wise to give that assistance. It has been pointed out that charters have been granted in the past containing conditions of expropriation. But, when the model Bill was framed, such a condition was left out, because it was well known that it was unnecessary, as parliament has the power to expropriate these enterprises at any time desired ; and. by putting in such clauses, you only handicap parliament, and, perhaps, injure the public interest. I think it is about time that the members of this House should recognize that the people of the country want the 63
development of this country's resources, and that they feel the need of railways for that purpose. Let us remove, in any proper way we can, any burden under which the people unjustly suffer, but, for the mere advancement of a seductive idea which, it may be, may work up to our practical disadvantage, let us not impose conditions which are different from those we have had, or which are to be found in other countries. I gather from the remarks of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), that if he were asked by a capitalist for his advice as a lawyer as to investing in an enterprise of this kind, he would say that this charter seemed to contain some unusual legislation, which might, as some members say, be harmless, but, on the whole, it would be better for the capitalist to have nothing to do with the matter. That is in accordance with the experience of every one who has tried to raise money upon the debentures or stock of any company such as this, whether chartered by the provincial or Dominion parliament. So, I do not see that any reasonable argument has been advanced why this Bill should be treated differently from any other Bill considered in this House. I am not prepared to say that the principle involved in the amendment is not a good thing, but it is one that should be most carefully considered before we adopt it, and, if it is deemed a wise policy, it should be adopted as a general policy and one applying to all roads. As to the enterprise itself, I do not think it is necessary to say anything. There are differences of opinion. If the parties interested in the district affected, and in the enterprise, can raise the money to develop that trade, It would be a great advantage to the city of Toronto, and, perhaps, a great advantage to the western country in giving a competing route for grain. If it is possible that this enterprise could be carried out, I say, in the name of all common sense, let us give these people the best possible Bill, and thus place them in a favourable position for floating the enterprise.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: I desire to say, for the sake of clearness, that if I thought a stipulation of this kind would handicap any railway, I would have a different opinion from that which I entertain. I do not see how it could, from any possible standpoint, handicap this railway or any other, because the valuation which is to be placed upon the road must be the full valuation of the road, including and taking into consideration its prospects in the future. Further than that, the valuation which would be placed upon the road for expropriation would be about 10 per cent more than its actual value if the ordinary rules of expropriation were carried out.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) a question ?

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I
would like to ask whether his opinion as a lawyer, is that the amendment would apply to the railway only or to the whole scheme, including the steamboats 7 Mr. GOURLEY. In the committee, we agreed that it should apply to both.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I
say, on the face of it, that it does not.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Speaking offhand, I should say all the property was included, because it uses the words ' undertaking and property.'

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will see that that is one of the difficulties. I am sure that no two lawyers in the House would agree upon the subject.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am not responsible for the opinion of any one else ;
I am giving my own opinion. My own opinion is that the words ' undertaking and property' mean exactly what they say. But, I would like to make myself clear with regard to this matter. I say that a provision of this kind is proper in the case of every railway declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. I limited my remarks to that. I think it is quite proper that this should be contained in a general Bill-I speak for myself in saying that. I say further, that the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland, Oxford) who has just sat down, seem to me to be destructive of his own argument. He tells us that a model Bill was agreed upon. Was it not as unfair to the companies first subjected to that Bill to be so treated as it is for this company to be made subject to this provision now ? The idea I suggested in the remarks I made was, that we should act upon this principle henceforth ; in other words, that we should insert a provision of this kind in a model Bill, a Bill which shall apply to all undertakings of this kind which are declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. The hon. gentleman will bear in mind that in making that statement I am not referring to the latter part of the amendment, because I do not concur with the principle of the second part of the amendment. I think that the second part of this amendment is not proper, and I will votr against the amendment as a whole unless that part is eliminated or modified.
I would suggest that some such modification as this be made, and I will then be prepared to vote for it:
But such subsidy shall not be deducted except to the extent by which such valuation is in excess of the cost of such property, together with a reasonable allowance for interest upon such cost.
If we have a provision of that kind I think the interests of the company would be perfectly safeguarded. As it stands at present I do not agree with it. I can seei that great injustice might be done to the!
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax.)
gentlemen who put thier money into this enterprise, if the amendment were adopted in the form in which it stands.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: We have spent some two hours upon this Bill, and I think the time has come that we should arrive at some conclusion upon it. The policy which 1 have always endeavoured to follow in matters of this kind has been that when legislation comes back; from the standing committees of this House, and especially from the Railway Committee, which is one of the most, if not the most, important, is invariably to support the report of the committee, unless it be shown that some error has been committed. When there is a divergence of opinion, as there is in the present instance, as to what is the best policy to be followed by the House, I have always thought it was best to support the committee and adopt their report. If we undertook to reopen a question that had been settled in the committee, we should have a great divergence of opinion, and it is doubtful whether this House or the committee are the best places for settling questions of this kind. We are accustomed to put a great deal of trust in the Railway Committee, and I think on this occasion we can safely adopt their report as the best judgment that can be placed upon the question. For this reason I am disposed to accept the report of the committee, especially in view of the fact that this very question has been debated at great length and threshed out by the committee. The argument which has impressed me most is that advanced by the hon. leader of the opposition. The hon. gentleman says : If you are to introduce this legislation why not do so by a model Bill 7 I may answer that some years ago, after a good deal of deliberation, we adopted a model Bill, this model Bill has been given to the committee to follow, and if we are to depart from the standing clauses which are to be found in this model Bill, it should be done only after due consideration. It should not be done in this Bill alone, but the new clauses to be introduced in the model Bill should be adopted by the Railway Committee itself and then be taken up by this House and adopted as the legislation of this country. I take much the same view as the leader 'of the opposition. He is not satisfied with the amendment which has been proposed, he would accept it in part but not in whole, and has proposed an amendment to the amendment. His amendment, I would suggest, would be at considerable variance with the policy we have hitherto followed. I am not prepared to say that it would not be in the right direction, but he will agree with me that before we adopt this amendment It should receive considerable attention from the Railway Committee. If it be thought proper to introduce new legislation of this character, for my part I would rather favour It.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: I was not proposing this as an amendment, but as simply voicing my own opinion.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I understand that, but it simply supports my contention that if amendments of that character are to be introduced at all they should be considered as part of a standard Bill. Coming-now to the amendment itself, it is in these words :
His Majesty shall have the right at any time to take over the undertaking and the property rights and franchises of the company

And for that purpose the Expropriation Act shall apply. We do not require to put that in any Bill. This parliament has the right at any time to expropriate railway property, the Canadian Pacific Railway, for instance.
I think my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) will agree with me that we have an undoubted right to do so, and we can do so to-morrow. I do not know but the time may come which my hon. friend from East York is sighing for, when we shall have all the railways of this country under our jurisdiction, when we shall have the ownership of them. I am not prepared to adopt his principle to-day, but some time we may come to his conclusion, we may do what has been done in other countries. But if that time ever came this parliament would have to consider the clauses of expropriation, what rule of expropriation should be followed. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition stated a moment ago that at the present time we have a certain rule of expropriation, that is to say, that we take the -value of the property as it is at the time we make the expropriation. We may expropriate a house which may have cost the owner $100,000, and we may only give for it $40,000 or even $20,000, as the marketable value of it at the time of expropriation. Whether we should have such a rule of expropriation as that to apply to railways is another matter. We should have to consider the question in all its details. I think on the whole the balance of opinion and of argument is that that rule should not apply in exceptional legislation under this Bill. But if there is to be exceptional legislation it ought to be carefully considered in a model Bill and not in a particular Bill.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
I wish to point out that we should never have had the confession that we have just listened to from the premier if this amendment had not been introduced to this Bill. He is coming to the *government ownership of railways. I totally disagree with the right hon. gentleman, however, in the doctrine that those things should be settled in the committees, and that parliament should not have a voice. We only delegate our rights to that committee, and we can review their action at any time ; if we see fit to supplement their action we have the right to do so. Another thing I wish to point out is that there are 634
no general principles underlying our legislation in this House. Our legislation in the past has been as erratic as a grasshopper's jumps. It jumps in every direction, and there are no general principles to be found. But we must begin some time. There is only one way to play upon the hornpipe and that is to play upon it, and you must -begin by playing upon it, and we propose to begin some time the policy of taking over these railways, and the sooner we begin the better. I hope the amendment as proposed here to-day will be adopted ; and I desire again to take this opportunity to compliment the right hon. gentleman on the slight confession he has made of his views in regard to government ownership of railways.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: I think the Prime Minister underestimates the importance of this discussion. We have discussed questions this session, hour after hour, not nearly so important as this one. I have heard the subject of transportation discussed here time after time, and I take this opportunity of explaining that while I have seconded this amendment, I am strongly in favour of bonuses to railways. I want bonuses for railways, and I will vote for railways through Ontario or through British Columbia and canals, too, if I am treated equally generously when I ask for railway subsidies in the county I have the honour to represent. I will vote for a dozen railways and canals, if they will enable us to take our share of the trade of this continent. Unless the Canadian people show more energy in the future than we have done in the past, we will never reach the position that God and nature intended us to fill. The people of Canada have been very glow during the last fifty years. If we had equalled the energy of our friends on the other side of the line, instead of having to-day a population of 6,000,000, we might have divided the population of the continent with them. While they have been building 200,000 miles of railway, equal to the railways of the whole world, we, little Canadians, sitting here, have built only 17,000 miles. There is the whole difference between the United States and Canada. They have built 200.000 miles of railway, equivalent to the railways of the whole globe, with the Canadian railways thrown in, They have conquered in their railway enterprises the sources of success, a success which is in direct ratio to the miles of railway they have built. We, little Canadians, sitting here-

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
Order, order.
Mr. GOURLEY-not fully comprehending our destiny, have missed great opportunities. I have heard gentlemen say in this House that we are at the end of our railway enterprises. If I believed that, I would lift my hat to Canada to-morrow and emigrate to

some more progressive country. We are only at the beginning of our railway building, and I hope in a few years to see the Georgian Bay canal built as well. We cannot allow the commerce of our country to go to the United States. I think if we doubled our national debt to-morrow, borrowed money at 2i per cent, expended it to build railways, not giving it to boodlers or contractors, but expended it honestly, it would be the greatest achievement Canada ever accomplished. Now, I just wanted to say this, in order to explain my position, in regard to my seconding this amendment, which otherwise might be misunderstood. Let me say one word more in reference to the principle which I think is involved in the amendment. The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) said that the principle ought to be made general. I agree with him, and I may say this, that in the Railway Committee I became alarmed at the trend of affairs; because I thought a most vicious principle was about to be introduced into the legislation of this country. Coming from the maritime provinces, I am not concerned about the rivalries of Ontario. I was only interested in seeing that the legislation of this parliament should not reflect upon the honour of the people. What I thought was going to happen in the Railway Committee was this :	I saw a large element in the
Railway Committee propounding the idea of requiring the subsidies to be paid back if we expropriated the railway. It is admitted that Canada has the power to expropriate, but, if we expropriated any railway, under any charter granted by this parliament, no lawyer, or honest man, would contend that we should take a dollar of the subsidies back unless notice to that effect was given in the charter. We have given no notice to the brokers, the bankers and the capitalists, who have taken our charter and given us their money, of our intentions in this respect.
The hon. member for Hants and other hon. gentlemen said : Do not put any notice in this charter ; we will fix it in the general Act. But, what would be the result ? This Act would be passed and the men who procured it would go to the brokers and bankers of London and get their money. No man would propose that any provision of the general Act should apply to that charter unless he were a criminal, or dishonest, unless that provision was already in the general Act, or passed concurrently with this. The difficulty is this ; If you are going to propose that the general Act shall apply to this company you are going to make the provision retroactive, and if you make it retroactive in reference to this company, you make it retroactive in reference to ' all companies, and the result would be that the reputation of Canada would suffer. I want to build 50.000 miles of railway in this country in the near future, and this is not the way to achieve such a result. While I Mr. GOURLEY.
agree with the hon. member for Hants, I agree with him only in so far as that the principle should be general. If it is to apply to this Bill, notice to the public should be given now. I do not agree with my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) that this is a private Bill. I have heard frequent discussion here about the transportation question, and it is a vital question, which must be settled ultimately, if the political power of this continent is to remain in Ottawa and not remain at Washington. When I looked at the map and saw that the route proposed by this Bill was going to cut off 300 miles and save us going round the peninsula of Ontario ; knowing what Canada's sentiments are in regard to the transportation of the products of the west, I concluded that this proposal was worth trying, because we want to try every solution for the settlement of this question. We have tried one system, but, if necessary, let us try another ; and, if the St. Lawrence canal system fails, let us build the Georgian Bay canal to-morrow. Let us build railways, until we do succeed in controlling the trade of this northern half of the continent. I hope the hon. gentlemen from Ontario and Quebec, when they talk about the transportation problem of this continent, will not hereafter think that everything begins at Collingwood on the one hand and ends at Quebec on the other. I would ask them to recollect, that when God made the ports of this country, that he made the ports of Halifax and St. John as well as the ports of Ontario and Quebec, and you people must try to recognize that we are legislating for the whole of Canada. I will vote money as readily for British Columbia or Ontario enterprises as I will for the construction of railways in the county in which I live. If I would not do that, I would be unworthy to occupy a seat in this parliament. When I hear hon. gentlemen talk about ending the transportation system at Collingwood on the one hand, or Quebec on the other, it strikes me as something that is not worthy of the discussions in this parliament. I propose, with the co-operation of my hon. friends from the maritime provinces, to introduce a discussion here, during the session, that will show some hon. gentlemen that the real transportation system of this continent will end at Halifax, and it is useless to talk about these little fresh water ports of Ontario and Quebec. You fresh water sailors up here appear to know very little about the ultimate possibilities of the transportation system of this young commercial giant of the north. If any hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, can show me that this amendment will interfere with the bringing of capital into this country, then, I am out of it. If this amendment will prevent this company financing this road, then, again, I am out of it. I want this road to be built, I do not care if there are fifty lines parallel to it. Let us try the experiment.

speechtext: When the contract was made with the Locomotive Works Company, at Kingston, Ont., for the construction of twenty locomotives, was there a clause inserted in it stipulating that the union rate of wages should be paid to the men employed in the works?

Mr. LaRIVIERE asked :
1. Has the following communication been received by the hon. the Minister of Agriculture from C. W. Peterson, secretary of the Territorial Horse Breeders' Association :-
' I am directed by the executive committee of the Territorial Horse Breeders' Association to call your attention to the fact that, although over 100,000 head of horses and mules have been purchased in the United States, and a considerable number in eastern Canada, for use in the South African campaign, for which satisfactory prices were paid, no attempt has apparently been made by the War Office authorities to secure any portion of this enormous number of remounts in the Territories, in spite of the fact that both the western contingents which left Canada for service in South Africa were mounted entirely on western horses, and that it has not been satisfactorily established that any difficulty was experienced in obtaining a sufficient number of a satisfactory type, although the notices given the rancher in both instances were entirely inadequate, owing to the hurried preparations.
It is well known to western breeders, and the fact is deeply deplored, that the impression evidently prevails in eastern Canada, that there are not enough horses raised in the Territories as yet for any practical purposes. This impression, however, is entirely erroneous. It is true that during the years of low values, breeding operations were largely discontinued, but it is also a fact that the absolute want Mr. BLAIR.
of a remunerative and stable market for horses of certain standard types, is not alone working a distinct hardship upon a vast number of small breeders, but it is also exerting a most baneful influence upon the development of the horse industry here, as it effectually discourages breeding operations. No person will for any length of time expend money and labour upon high class breeding stock without a reasonable assurance of ultimate satisfactory financial returns from his efforts.
Vast portions of the North-west Territories present such topographical, meteorological and soil conditions that general farming or cattleraising can never be successfully prosecuted therein. Such being the case, it necessarily follows that these enormous areas must eventually be devoted, if utilized at all, to the raising of horses, or, in the more favourable localities, to sheep-raising. It is, therefore, clear that the business of horse-raising must perforce ultimately develop into one of the most important branches of agriculture in the west. But even if these circumstances were not in themselves sufficient to bring horse-breeding operations prominently to the front in the Territories, the local conditions are such that no horse-producing country in the world could successfully compete against our cheap pastures rich in lime, and favourable climate, enabling horses to range out winter and summer, at little or no expense to the owner.
The present position of affairs is simply unbearable, and I am directed by my committee to urge you, as emphatically as lies in my power, to come to the rescue of our breeders in some way. The market for heavy draught horses is all that could be desired at present, but the conditions here are not nearly so favourable to the production of this class of horses as to the raising of light horses, and it is particularly in connection with the latter that government assistance is needed.
After devoting considerable thought to the matter, I am directed by my committee to suggest, as a feasible means of putting this industry on a proper footing, that your department should deal with it somewhat on the same basis as has been adopted in respect to the dairy industry in the Territories. An amount of money might be appropriated at the forthcoming session of parliament, sufficient to enable you to purchase, as an experiment, a limited number of horses in the west, conforming to the cavalry, artillery and mounted infantry standards, at a fair minimum price. At least two months' notice should be given to breeders here of the dates and places where your agent would purchase, and also full information respecting the types of horses required, and to what extent they would be handled. The association would undertake to look after the local organization, advertising, &c., and would otherwise render your department every assistance possible. Ample notice is absolutely essential, as horses are usually ranging out, and it takes considerable time to get them in and properly handled. This will not, under ordinary circumstances, be done until there is a sale in sight. Three months' notice would be better than two. In the meantime, negotiations could be opened up with the remount department of the British War Office, with a view to having a purchasing officer sent out, as soon as your department had gathered a sufficient number of horses, to inspect them and select all those coming up to the army standards.
There would doubtless be a certain number of culls no matter how carefully the horses had
been purchased; but those would, in centres like Toronto, Montreal or Ottawa, in most cases, be worth nearly as much as your department paid for them, and if the prices offered territorial breeders for their animals were fixed at their approximate value for army purposes, less the cost of transportation and other expenses (which would still leave a very satisfactory figure), it is unlikely that any considerable loss would be sustained by your department in the whole transaction. Any trifling debit balance would, of course, be amply justified by the impetus which would be given horse-breeding operations in the Territories.
Even granting that the necessary financial arrangements could be made to enable this association to successfully handle such a scheme itself, it could not hope to do so as economically and efficiently as could be done by the federal government. You have in the person of the live stock commissioner an official well fitted to do the organization work required. At every considerable point in the Territories there is a mounted police divisional headquarters where assistance could be obtained in purchasing, holding and shipping these animals, and where an experienced veterinarian in the employ of the department would be available. In fact, the cost of handling the scheme in the hands of your department could be reduced to a mere minimum.
It is anticipated that if an arrangement such as outlined could be continued for five or six years under a government guarantee, the production of military remounts in the Territories would easily double, and if proper representations were made to the Imperial government, based upon actual knowledge of the number *of suitable horses available annually and the record for endurance and constitution which western horses would, by that time, undoubtedly have made for themselves in the service, it should prove a feasible proposition to induce the War Office authorities to establish regular remount depots at various points throughout the west, such as are now maintained in the Argentine Republic by the British government in connection with the Indian army.
In conclusion, I am to express, in behalf of my committee, that its representations may meet with favourable consideration at your
hands.'	, ,.	.
