speakername: The AIINISTER OF CUSTOAIS (Hon. Wm. Paterson) :

speechtext:
House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Hon. Air. Fielding :
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into committee to consider of the Ways and Means for raising the Supply to be granted to His Majesty; and the proposed motion of Mr. Borden (Halifax) in amendment thereto.
['I do not think it will be possible. It would be better to understand that it will close on Thursday.']

Air. Speaker, when a vote is challenged on the motion to go into Committee of Ways and means, the question that faces a

member of this House is not alone whether the policy of the government of the day is satisfactory, but also whether the member prefers the policy of the government or the policy propounded by hon. gentlemen on the opposition benches. And, on this occasion, the duty devolving upon a member of the House is made simpler by the fact that the leader of the opposition has condensed the policy of himself and his following in the shape of the amendment which is now be-foi'e the House. As a further means of ascertaining exactly and entirely what is the policy of the opposition, we also have before us the speeches of members of the opposition, and, Sir, I think that any one who lias followed the reports of the debate up to this stage must have been astonished at the impossible positions which our friends on the opposition benches endeavour to maintainor would be astonished but for the fact that our friends have been endeavouring to maintain these positions for the last four or five years, and our astonishment now merges into a feeling of amusement. At once they tell us that the policy of the government involves too high protection, involves excessive duties, at least they complain that too much money is taken from the pockets of the people by the tariff that is in force, and at the same time they complain that the tariff is not high enough, and they think it necessary to place that view in the form that is now before us. In one breath they complain that the government of the day has been and is guilty of dreadful extravagance, but 1 notice that they entirely fail now, as they have failed in the last five years to take any practical exception to any material portion of the expenditures proposed by the government. As I say, in one breath they tell us that the Liberal party as represented by the government in this House is keeping in force the obsolete protective system which was inaugurated in 1878 and maintained until 1896. They tell us that the protective system is still in force, but at the same time they deem it necessary to frame and present an amendment, which, I think at all events, nails them to the position that the present tariff is not high enough. They bring in an amendment which, I suppose, they will support, and they will then feel free to to go out into the country and appeal to the manufacturers on the ground that the tariff in force is not sufficiently protective, and they will make the promise to the manufacturers that if the country will give them the opportunity they will put in force a tariff that will be properly protective. In one breath they tell us that the policy of the present administration is not a proper, a judicious policy; and, in the same breath, they tell us that the administration is simply applying the old policy which the Conservative party maintained in this country for something like eighteen years. In other words, they complain that the Liberal party has stolen the Conservatives clothes. They seem to wish to complain that the members of the Liberal party have become converted to Conservative doctrine. Admitting, for the moment, that that is true, is there any good reason for any patriotic Conservative to complain on that score ? If a Conservative really believes that the principle of protection is a proper principle and that it should be applied in this country, is there any real reason why he should complain because a member of the Liberal party, or an Independent or any other citizen becomes a convert to what he himself, at all events, believes to be the true political gospel ? Liberals, I think, have never urged such a complaint as this. In years past in this country there were contests over questions of principle. Something like sixty or seventy years ago there was a contest in this country on the question of responsible government. The Whigs contended for the principle of responsible government, and the Tories contended against that principle. Time went on and by-and-by the Tories became converted to the principle of responsible government. And, so far as I have been able to learn there never was a Liberal who complained of any Tory who became a convert.
The last hon. gentleman who occupied the floor in this debate, speaking last Friday evening, it seemed to me tried to include in his speech nearly all the impossible positions which the opposition attempts to maintain on the fiscal question. There have been hon. gentlemen on the other side who have taken one line of argument, and gentlemen who have taken a different line. But the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) himself managed to take both lines of argument. He proved, I suppose to his own satisfaction at all events, that the claim that is made by the government that there was a surplus in the last fiscal year of some $8,-
000.000 was an entirely mistaken claim. He proved to his own satisfaction that, instead of there being a surplus, there was a deficit, that the people of the country at the end of the last fiscal year were in a worse position than at the commencement of the year. And this, notwithstanding the fact, that, as I understand it, the public debt was reduced by $779,000 in the fiscal year. A short time after, he proved-also, I suppose to his own satisfaction-that the government took out of the pockets of the people $8,000,000 in excess of what was required to meet the expenses of the country. He also presented a considerable array of figures to prove that the system of protection was still in force and to prove that considerable duties were still in force in regard to agricultural products. He was, at that timb, endeavouring to give an answer to a question. that had been asked from this side of the House. Some hon. gentleman on this side had invited any member of the opposition or any one else who believed in the principle of protection to show how the

agriculturist and how the labour of this country might be protected. The hon. member for South Simcoe took up the tariff and showed that on a number of agricultural products, a considerable tariff was still in force. But that did not prove to me that these articles are protected or that the farmers reap any benefit from the protection of the tariff which is in force on those articles. For instance, there is a duty of 12 cents a bushel on wheat-I think that is the rate. But I feel certain that there is not one farmer in a hundred in this country who gets any advantage through that duty upon wheat. The mere fact that there is a duty upon wheat does not at all prove that the farmer who grows wheat receives any advantage from the tariff. But the hon. member had satisfied himself that the agricultural produce of the country was protected, and in the next breath he told us that after the Liberal government came into power they almost entirely wiped out the duties that had been previously levied upon the imported products of the United States, and had then gone down to Washington and asked for some reciprocity arrangements.
But there were some hon. gentlemen opposite who made a fair argument, and observed some logic in their reasoning. It appeared to me that one of the most logical speeches that I heard coming from the opposition benches was that of the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), who declared himself a protectionist and against the present tariff, because it does not afford sufficient protection. He told the House, what is a fact, that of the $189,000,000 worth of imports brought into this country last year, $76,000,000 of that total represented free goods. As to that fact, the hon. member for East Toronto and myself are in entire agreement, but our conclusions from the same fact differ pretty widely. That hon. gentleman declared that the tariff was bad so far as it involved this free trade principle ; while I believe the tariff is good so far as it contains that principle. He stated that the people of Canada, by a very large majority, were opposed to the introduction of free trade principles into our tariff, and on that point also I cannot agree with him. I think, and certainly hon. gentlemen of the opposition are of this opinion, because they constantly charge the government with failure to obey the mandate,- that in the year 1898 the people of Canada gave a mandate against the principle of protection in our tariff ; it is my opinion, but possibly there is room for a little disagreement, that in the year 1900 the people of Canada again gave a mandate against the application of the principle of protection in our tariff. At all events, the opposition, in complaining against the height of our tariff and then complaining that it is too low, must be considered as holding an untenable position.
One complaint I have to make against the amendment submitted by the leader of Mr. SCOTT.
the opposition is, that ic is not definite enough. It is framed in terms vague enough, I fear, to permit gentlemen representing that party to go through the country later on and make divers appeals to the people, similar to those divers appeals that they made last fall, when the people of Canada were asked to decide as between the Liberal and Conservative parties. We know that members of the opposition, and even leaders of the party, went through different parts of the country making entirely different pleas and entirely different promises. In one province, for instance, they promised to have a duty put on lumber, while, on the other hand, in other parts of the country, they were complaining against the small duty at present existing upon some classes of lumber. In the province of Manitoba, so prominent a leader as Hugh John Macdonald, for instance, promised that if the Conservative party was returned to power the farmers would be given the advantage of free agricultural implements ; while, in other provinces, other Conservative leaders, among them Sir Charles Tupper and the Hon. Mr. Foster, made definite promises that if the Conservative party was returned to power the duty on agricultural implements would be increased. I give these instances as an illustration of the various tactics that -were resorted to, and the various promises that were made by the different Conservative leaders last fall in various parts of the country. In the part of the country from which I come, the government was assailed because its leader was a Frenchman and a Roman Catholic. I state this without fear of successful contradiction, although I notice that since this session opened and since this debate began, certain prominent gentlemen on the other side have questioned whether it were true that racial and religious cries were resorted to by members of the opposition. I say that in the part of the country from which I come the electors were appealed to on the ground that the leader of the Liberal party, and some of his lieutenants, were Frenchmen and Roman Catholics. I believe it is a fact also, that in the province of Quebec, the Liberal party were attacked because one of the leaders was ' too British for me.' Now. I say that I take issue with this amendment partly because it is not definite enough, and I take issue with it because it means, if it means anything, that the principle of protection in the present tariff ought to be increased. I take issue with the amendment because it means, if it means anything, that duties should be increased on agricultural implements, and that duties should be reimposed on such articles as binder twine, barbed wire and cream separators, many of which are used by the farmers in our part of the country. I take issue with it because it means, if it means anything, that the duties at present in force should be increased in respect to the whole line of articles which may be imported into
this country. As I said at the commencement, the question that faces me is not entirely whether I deem the policy at present in force as satisfactory, for if I were obliged to give a candid opinion, I would have to say that I am not entirely satisfied with the tariff of the government as it stands, and any dissatisfaction I may have with regard to it is on account of the height of the duties imposed under that tariff. I notice that the Finance Minister, in his statement, partly foreshadowed a lessening of the revenues reaped under the tariff at present in force.
I have a specific to recommend if there is danger of a lessening of the revenue and the specific that I would recommend is to make a further cut in! the tariff. I believe that in regard to some articles the tariff at present is to a certain extent protective, and I believe, too, that a protective tariff cannot be called a revenue tariff. If the tariff protects a certain line of manufactures it is a tariff which is not calculated to bring in a revenue. So, I would say that if there is to be feared a lessening of revenue under the present tariff, the proper way to obviate the danger is to make further cuts In that tariff. I will give an illustration from the tariff history of the country. Up to 1894 a protective tariff, a tariff of 35 per cent was levied against agricultural Implements coming into this country, and in 1894 a reduction was made to 20 per cent on mowers and binders, a reduction equal to 43 per cent. Since that time the revenue has not lessened notwithstanding that the duty was cut almost in two. The revenue has not lessened, but, on the contrary, it has Increased to an extent equal to nearly 500 per cent. In 1894, before the reduction and while there was a duty of 35 per cent, the revenue reaped from hinders was 824,478.50. Last year, under a 20 per cent tariff, the revenue that was reaped was $160,860.40. Upon mowers, in 1894, when a, 35 per cent duty was levied, the revenue reaped was $9,935.65. In 1900 under a 20 per cent tariff, the revenue was $71,111.40. The revenue reaped from the whole line of agricultural implements in 1894 was $77,921.86. Since 1894 the duties not only upon binders and mowers have been cut, but on other agricultural implements they have been cut from, I think, 35 to 25 per cent, and in 1900, under these lower duties, there was a revenue reaped, not of $77,921.86, hut of no less than $357,200.22, Carrying this argument a little further we find that there has been a general cut in the taxation on all articles brought in since 1897 of from 10 to 121 per cent and that this cut was followed, not by a reduction of revenue, but, by an increase of customs duties of about 40 per cent or an increase from $20,000,000 to $28.000 000. So the argument that is advanced bv the opposition Is fallacious : the mere fact that there has been an increase in the
revenue, in the amount of money that the people have paid in customs duties, is not proof positive that any greater taxation has been levied, because, in regard to binders and mowers, while the amount of revenue which reached tihe coffers of the country was vastly larger this last year than in 1S94, the fact must be plain that no additional taxation was imposed upon the people, or upon the farmers who purchased these agricultural implements, but, that on the contrary, there has been a marked lessening of taxation. While tlm rate of taxation was 35 per cent and while it did not yield money to the general revenues of the country, it was still levied upon the people ; it did not come into the treasury of Canada, but it went into the pockets of "the manufacturers. I take issue with the amendment when it strikes at the preferential arrangement that is now in force between this country and the mother country. I may say that personally 1 do not feel so much interest in whether the preferential arrangement is of advantage to the people of Great Britain as in whether it is of advantage to the people of Canada.
It is because I believe that the preferential arrangement has been of great advantage to the people of Canada in lessening the taxation imposed upon our people that I stand by the preferential arrangement as It is at present upon the statute-book. ^ Before 'I sit down I Wish to refer briefly to another question that is not allied with the trade or tariff issue, but which is a financial question, and which, I think, may be properly mentioned and discussed in this debate. It is not now, and I trust may not become, a matter at issue between the political parties. I allude to that coming Change in relations between the North-west Territories of Canada and this parliament, and as I say that is a question largely financial and so I think it is not out of place in this discussion. I shall preface the remarks that I have to make by the statement that I take it as a tribute to the far-sightedness and the statesmanship of the gentlemen who, in I860, met in the city of Quebec and framed the arrangement which resulted in the confederation of the provinces of Upper find Lower Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, that, in the portion of the country which they then contemplated should become a part of Canada-I allude to the North-west Territories which at that time were known as Rupert's Land-there has hover since the North-west became a part of Canada, and not up to this time, been a thought, or a suggestion, in the mind of any person in that country, so far as their future was concerned 'Other than of becoming a province of the Dominion of Canada and a permanent part of confederation. Notwithstanding the fact that, in som e respects some people there may believe that it would be to their immediate material advantage to be associated in a different way with the country Immediately to the south so that they might

trade with the cities of St. Paul, Minneapolis, and Chicago, which are much nearer than the cities of Toronto and Montreal, Where they chiefly trade, notwithstanding that materially and immediately it might he, in a way, to their advantage to look to a different destiny, there is not at the present time, never h-as been, and I do not think ever will be any thought in the mind of any resident, or any citizen of the Northwest, but to remain as a part of confederation and a part of the Dominion of Canada. The people in that country have for some years been looking forward to the time when a change should be made and when the part of the country in which they live should become in all respects equal to the other provinces of the Dominion.
Occasionally, in this House-even since this session has opened-there have been remarks dropped which might lead a western member to believe that the opinion is held down here that the western people are very impatient ; that they are looking for . their wrongs to be righted immediately ; that they want things to move a little too fast ; but, Sir, in regard to this question the people of the North-west cannot be accused of any undue baste. They have been heretofore working under such a constitution as the Federal parliament thought well to grant. They have now come to a stage when they feel that some additional powers are required and when some different arrangement ought be made so as to enable them to better carry on the work of local government. The difficulty they labour under is not so much constitutional as it is financial. So far as their constitutional powers are concerned the people feel that they might possibly get along for some time yet without any marked change. But they have come to a point in their history when they feel hampered as regards their finances. The members of the House all know the difference which exists between the financial relations of the provinces to the Dominion and the financial relations of the North-west Territories to the Dominion. Each of the provinces has a fixed financial status and the provincial subsidies are not voted by this parliament year after year, but are paid under statute, whereas with regard to the North-west Territories the grant which corresponds in a sense to the provincial subsidies, has to be voted each session by this House. To better explain some of the difficulties which arise under the present system, I will quote the words of the chief spokesman of the Northwest Territories, the Hon. Mr. Hauitain, from a speech he made in the legislature last session. He said :
already exhausted every means of obtaining any very large increase to that parliamentary vote. Even were any government so well disposed towards the Territories-and I think all governments are in a way-the conditions surrounding a parliamentary vote, the conditions which exist at Ottawa, prevent any adequate amount being given to us under our present institutions. I make that statement believing such to be the case. So long as the Territories remain in a dependent condition and receive their financial assistance as a matter of grace rather than of right; so long as the Territories remain in the position of having a large amount of money voted as_ a grant in addition to a number of other things which the provinces do for themselves, provided for them every year in the Dominion Supply, just for so long will it be impossible for the Territories to secure that suitable financial recognition without which even the present institutions cannot be successfully carried on. We have pretty well passed through the preliminary stages, and we have pretty well come to an end of our usefulness so far as our present condition will permit us. We have to a certain extent fairly well exhausted, in the broader sense of the word, the powers given to us under the legislative jurisdiction which we now possess. I believe the time has come for beginning the superstructure for which we have been laying the foundations. I believe we have laid these foundations well; and that so far as the institutions we have created; so far as the main body of our laws-which deal not only with the primary but even with many of the secondary wants and interests of this country-are concerned, I believe we have a good body of laws, and that very largely we have exhausted the more obvious uses and powers of the constitution which we have and of the powers which we possess under it. X do not say that further progress is impossible, but I do say that any very large amount of progress, or any very large amount of development, is not possible under the existing institutions.
I will not take up time arguing that the North-west Territories have pretty nearly arrived at a period in their history when a change must be made in their existing relations to the Federal parliament. The people up there, at least if they are properly represented in the legislature and if their chief spokesman the Prime Minister of the Territories, is to be relied upon ; the people there have come to the conclusion that very shortly some change will have to be looked for. Before the local elections in 1S98, the Hon. Mr. Hauitain spoke at various points throughout the Territories on this subject, and I shall quote from the language he used at one place to show that even three years ago this change was looked forward to and that the present legislature of the Territories was in reality given a mandate to open up negotiations with respect to the subject. Speaking at Yorkton, the Hon. Mr. Hauitain said :
We might well go on developing under the territorial system for a long time to come if our revenue would only keep pace with our requirements. But the present financial condition is an impossible one-I mean the condition of being *dependent upon the annual vote of parliament tor the larger part of our income. We have

If the financial question is capable of other solution, I will be satisfied to remain as at present. The only thing there seems to be to do is to think at least of negotiating for provincial establishment. I feel convinced that it will be the principal work of the new legislature before the end of its four years' term to enter into such negotiations. With the

greater development that now seems assured, the needs in respect of schools and improvement will certainly develop. Outside of direct taxation, there seems no possibility of a solution except by provincial establishment-not perhaps to-day or next year, but in the reasonably near future.
Last session in the legislature the following address was voted upon by all the local representatives of the people and unanimously adopted :
1.	Whereas by the British North America Act,
1867,	it was (amongst other things) enacted that it should be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice of Her Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, on address from the Houses of the parliament of Canada, to admit Rupert's Land and the North-west Territory, or either of them, into the union on such terms and conditions in each case as should be in the addresses expressed and as the Queen should think fit to approve, subject to the provisions of the said Act ;
2.	And whereas, by an address from the Houses of the parliament of Canada Her Majesty was prayed to unite Rupert's Land and the North-west Territory with the Dominion of Canada ;
3.	And whereas, in order to further the petition of the parliament of Canada, Her Majesty, under the authority of the Rupert's Land Act,
1868,	accepted a surrender from the governor and company of adventurers of England trading into Hudson's bay, of all the lands, territories, rights, privileges, liberties, franchises, powers and authorities whatsoever granted or purported to be granted by certain letters patent therein recited to the said company in Rupert's Land ;
* 4. And whereas, in the said address it was represented to Her Majesty, as a reason for the extension of the Dominion of Canada westward, that the welfare of the population of these territories would be materially enhanced by the formation therein of political institutions, bearing analogy, as far as circumstances will admit, to those which existed in the several provinces then forming the Dominion ,*
5.	And whereas, the Houses of the parliament of Canada by their said address expressed to Her Majesty their willingness to assume the duties and obligations of government and legislation as regards these territories ;
6.	And whereas, in pursuance and exercise of the powers invested in the Queen by the aforesaid Acts, Her Majesty, by and with the advice of her most honourable Privy Council, ordered and declared that from and after the 15th day of July, 1870, Rupert's Land and the North-western Territory should be admitted into and become part of the Dominion of Canada, and granted power and authority to the parliament of Canada to legislate for the future welfare and good government of these territories ;
7.	And whereas, by the British North America Act, 1871, the parliament of Canada was further given power from time to time to make provision for the administration, peace, order and good government of any territory not for the time being included in any province;
8.	And whereas, under the several authorities so given, the parliament of Canada has created political institutions in these territories bearing a close analogy i.o those which exist in the several provinces of the Dominion ;
9.	And whereas, by the confederation compact the provinces which formed the Dominion, on
the 15th day of July, 1870, were furnished with the means of carrying on local self-government upon certain well-defined bases ;
10.	And whereas, the territories, being an integral part of the . Dominion, and having had imposed upon them the duties and obligations incidental to the political institutions which have been given to them, and which said duties and obligations the parliament of Canada has declared its willingness to assume, are entitled to such Federal assistance for their maintenance as will bear due proportion and analogy to that given to other portions of the Dominion for similar purposes;
11.	And whereas, repeated representations have been made in various ways to the government of Canada with the view of obtaining just and equitable financial assistance towards providing for the proper and efficient administration of local affairs in the Territories and for the public necessities of their rapidly increasing population ;
12.	And whereas, such representations have been met by intermittent and insufficient additions to the annual grant, the provision so made by the parliament of Canada never bearing any adequate proportion to the financial obligations imposed by the enlargement and development of the political institutions created by itself;
13.	And whereas, it is desirable that a basis should be established upon which the- claims of the Territories to suitable financial recognition may be settled and agreed upon :
14.	Therefore be it resolved, that an humble address to His Excellency the Governor General be adopted by this House praying him that he will be pleased to cause the fullest enquiry to be made into the position of the Territories, financial and otherwise, and to cause such action to be taken as will provide for their present and immediate welfare and good government, as well as the due fulfilment of the duties and obligations of government and legislation assumed, with respect to these Territories, by the parliament of Canada ;
15.	And be it further resolved that, whereas,
by the British North America Act, 1871, it was (amongst other things) enacted that the parliament of Canada may from time to time establish new provinces in any territories forming for the time being part of the Dominion of Canada, but not included in any province thereof, and may, at the time of such establishment, make provision for the constitution and administration of ...	. such province, His Excellency be also prayed to order inquiries to be made and accounts taken with a view to the settlement of the terms and conditions upon which the territories or any part thereof shall be established as a province, and that before any such province is established, opportunity should be given to the people of the territories, through their accredited representatives, of considering and discussing such terms and conditions.
That, Sir, is the succinct record of the history and the present claims of the legislature of the North-west Territories. And that the government here have been fairly seized of the fact that a change in the near future will be necessary. I infer from a statement that has been made in this House by one of the ministers of the Crown since the commencement of the present session, in answer to a question that was put by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean). The hon. member for East

York asked if any new provinces were likely to be formed in the North-west Territories after the census was taken, and this answer was given by the 'Minister of the Interior :
A deputation, consisting of two members of the North-west government, Mr. Haultain and Mr. Ross, were in Ottawa some time ago on other business, and took the opportunity of discussing this question. I may say that while during the last three or four years they have not addressed any official communication to the government, yet from time to time they have discussed with myself and my colleagues the question of giving the Territories provincial status, and lately they handed us a memorandum on that subject. We have not officially replied to that memorandum as yet, hut expect to do so shortly. This is a matter, of course, requiring serious consideration. I may say, in a general way, that I am of the opinion that it will have to be dealt with in the very near future. The people of the Territories are as capable of self-government as any other people In Canada, and have shown their fitness by the admirable manner in which they have carried on their present administration. Of course, the financial question is a serious one. The subsidy required for the Territories in the course of a few years would have to be greatly increased, and there is the question of the control of public lands and matters of that kind which would have to be settled.
These various statements will obviate any necessity of my going into the question as to whether the time has come for this change. The representatives of the Territories think the time is approaching, and we may conclude from this statement of the Minister of the Interior that the government here are seized of the fact that the time is rapidly approaching when a change must be made in the relations of the North-west legislature to this parliament ; and as the census is to be taken this year, the data thus obtained will make it possible to intelligently negotiate, and will bring a favourable time for commencing negotiations.
I may refer briefly to the causes which make this change necessary. A country so large as the North-west Territories, with a sparse population, is always an expensive country to govern locally. During the last few years very material additions have been made to the population. Immigrants have been coming into the country in large numbers, making necessary further expenditures on education and public works. I believe that in one year as many as one hundred new school districts have been formed in the North-west Territories, and have had to be provided for by the local government. No argument is necessary to show that with such a condition of affairs the financial requirements of the local government are increasing very rapidly. As to the way in which the local authorities expend their money, statistics show that a very large proportion of their revenues is devoted to education and public works. The total amount at the disposal of the local legislature last year was $470,000. Of this, no less than $182,000 was voted for education and Mr. SCOTT.
$178,000 for public works, including the construction of roads and bridges, sinking public wells, providing ferries and similar services, leaving only $110,00b for civil government, legislation, administration of civil justice, and so forth. In these figures I think we find full justification for the commendatory remarks made by the Minister of the Interior with reference to the territorial government.
I wish to refer for a moment to a question that has been raised with respect to some of the foreign settlers. The hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) asked a question in the House as to the provision being made for the education of the Doukhobors, a considerable number of whom are settled in the Territories, I assume from the manner of his question that he thought the government should devote a certain amount of money and take certain steps to see that the education of the Doukhobors was not neglected. I have not any very intimate knowledge of that subject, but I am aware that the members of the local government have had conferences with representatives of those people ; and while I believe that there is and will be a considerable amount of difficulty with regard to the education of the Doukhobors, owing- to their peculiar customs and beliefs, still I think that the past history of the local government gives us warrant to believe that that government is perfectly competent to deal with whatever difficulty may exist.
Hon. members will readily understand that in a part of the country to which many foreign immigrants are coming year after year-and since the opening up of the Northwest Territories, every year there has been an influx of a large number of people who may be classed as foreigners, people from the continent of Europe,-there must be problems of more or less difficulty to be solved by the local authorities. In the past, the local government has been found competent to cope with the difficulties which have arisen, and while a certain amount of patience may be required in dealing with peculiar people like the Doukhobors, we may take it for granted that the local government will be competent to grapple with any difficulties that may arise. I fear that the local authorities would take exception, and properly, to this parliament stepping into the domain of education, the power of dealing with which was many years ago conferred upon the local government. The difficulty of dealing with people like the Doukhobors, owing to their peculiarities, this House, of course, has a right to consider, and the consideration will further impress on hon. members the necessity of providing financial means to the local government to enable it to deal effectively and efficiently with these people.
I propose, Sir, with the permission of the House, to glance very briefly at the political history of the North-west Territories. The
acquisition of these territories was contemplated by the statesmen who met in Quebec in 1865-the fathers of confederation ; and from one of the resolutions then passed, I extract the following sentence :
Provision being made for tlie admission, on equitable terms, of Newfoundland, the Northwest Territories, British Columbia and Vancouver, on such terms as the parliament 'Of the federated provinces shall deem equitable land as shall receive the assent of Her Majesty.
Respecting the contention that the expenditures incurred with regard to the Northwest Territories, including the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, should be wholly charged against the North-west Territories, let me quote another portion of the resolution as showing the view on this point held by the fathers of confederation :
The communication with the North-west Territories and the improvements required for the development of the trade of the great west with the seaboard, are regarded by this conference as subjects of the highest importance to the federated provinces.
Thus, the view held by the fathers of confederation respecting the expenditures which would have to be made in the North-west Territories, was that these expenditures would not be incurred so much for the Northwest Territories as for the provinces which originally formed confederation. The territory was acquired following an address from the Canadian parliament to Her Majesty, praying that Rupert's Land and the North-west Territories might be united to the Dominion of Canada. The address recited that:
It would promote the prosperity of the Canadian people and conduce to the advantage of the whole empire, if the Dominion of Canada constituted under the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867, were extended westward to the shores of the Pacific ocean. That the colonization of the fertile lands of the Saskatchewan, the Assiniboine and the Red river districts; the development of the mineral wealth which abounds in the region of the North-west, and the extension of commercial intercourse through the British possessions in America from the Atlantic to the Pacific, are alike dependent on the establishment of a stable government for the maintenance of law and order in the North-western Territory; and that the welfare of a sparse and widely scattered population of British subjects of European origin, already inhabiting these remote and unorganized territories, would he materially enhanced by the formation therein of political institutions bearing analogy, as far as circumstances will admit, to those which exist in the several provinces of this Dominion.
The foregoing quotations show distinctly, first, that the North-west Territories were acquired for the benefit primarily of the confederated provinces ; second, that it was the intention of Canada to extend to the Territories a system of government bearing analogy to those of the provinces; and third, they include a guarantee that the Territories would be placed on an equitable basis compared with the other provinces. That
I take to mean that we would eventually be given a constitutional and financial position, which would bear strict analogy to the positions occupied by each one of the other provinces. On the 15th July, 1870, the North-west Territories were admitted into confederation and became part and parcel of the Dominion. The history of the local government in that country since .then I shall not take up the time of the House by going over, I may say briefly, that from time to time additional powers were conferred on the local authorities until now there is very little difference-practically none constitutionally-between the position of the Territories and that of any province. The Territories lack a few of the powers possessed by the provinces, as, for instance, the power to borrow money on the public credit, the power to charter railways, tlie power to erect and maintain such institutions as insane asylums. But they have authority over education and other matters; and so far as any power has been conferred upon them, they exercise it in exactly the same manner as similar powers are exercised out toy the local legislatures and governments in provinces.
I do not wish to go into any of the details at present. My intention is merely to draw the attention of parliament to a subject with which this parliament will almost certainly have to deal in the very near future-almost certainly before the end of this term. But there are one or two details to which I wish to refer briefly. The question will arise whether one or more provinces should be created out of the present territories, namely, the two Assiniboias, Saskatchewan and Alberta. On that point I do not care to offer any decided opinion, and I do not know that there exists in the minds of the people any very decided opinion. My personal opinion is in favour of the erection of only one province, as I think it would be a mistake to create too many governments in that country, and X believe that one system-one lieutenant governor and one executive-would be sufficient to attend to the interests of local government in that country. The point is sometimes raised that the area is very large, which no one will dispute, but it is not larger than that of at least one existing province. The area of the four districts in the North-west Territories is about 302,000 miles, and that of the province of British Columbia comprises 383,000 square miles. The area is not very much larger than the area of Ontario, which is 222,000 square miles, and of Quebec, which is 228,000 square miles.
It is interesting in this connection, to remember that, prior to confederation the late Sir John Macdonald held strongly to the opinion that a legislative union for all Canada would be preferable to a federal union. If a man so far-sighted as Sir John Macdonald believed that the legislative interests of all Canada might be most satisfactorily

dealt with by one legislature sitting at Ottawa, and if that proposition was possible, the proposition that the area comprised in these four districts could be governed in a local sense by one legislature is not at all an absurdity. Another suggestion has been mooted, one on which I have no hesitation in expressing a very decided opinion-a suggestion that a portion of the territory should be annexed to the province of Manitoba. The people of the Territories generally, would very strongly oppose the carrying out of such a proposition; and the people who, if it were carried out would find themselves in the province of Manitoba, would and do most strongly oppose the proposition. As 1 have explained, the relations at present existing between the legislature of the Territories and this parliament, and the whole constitutional and financial position of the Territories limit the resources of local government practically to the annual grants voted by this parliament, apart from the powers of direct taxation which have been conferred upon it. I do not imagine that this House would look with equanimity upon the powers of direct taxation being applied to any severe extent in that country. This House looks to a speedy settlement of that country, looks for a large immigration to that country, looks for progress in that country, and certainly the application of the power of direct taxation to a severe extent would not conduce to that progress or that early settlement or any very large immigration. Apart from the power of direct taxation, really the only resource of the local government of the territory is the annual grant voted by this parliament. I do not wish to complain that the annual grants have not been fairly generous, although in no year have they sufficed to fully and adequately meet the requirements. Looked at from all points of view, however, I think the yearly grants have been fairly generous. But a position has been reached where the need is growing so fast year by year that it is found almost impossible or entirely impossible to get the income from this parliament which is necessary. I will not weary the House with a statement of what the annual grant has been-that may be found in the estimates for the various years, which are on record. I will not go any further into the matters of detail, but shall draw the attention of the House to what X think should be a broad, general principle upon which the arrangements which will be made should be negotiated and arrived at. On the constitutional side, I imagine, the proposition is very simple. I have no doubt that this House will very readily confer upon the legislature of the Territories all the powers which have been conferred upon the legislatures of the provinces. But financially the case may be more complex. On the financial side there may be room for argument. Financially, the various pro-

be kept in this country instead of one. There is no practical reason why the same work should not be done by us as is done by the Attorney General's Department in the provinces. We should also have control of the registry offices. The important power to legislate with regard to property and' civil rights given to us in one section of the North-west Territories Act is largely curtailed by the Dominion parliament having undertaken to deal with the question of land titles under the Land Titles Act, and I need not remind the House how often we run up against the Land Titles Act in attempting to legislate on many questions. In much of our important legislation we have to deal with land and land titles, and it is a practical argument that if we had the power-as they have in the provinces-to deal exclusively with property and civil rights we should be able to make a great many improvements in much of our general legislation as well as Improvements in the land titles system itself. I believe the land titles system under local administration can be made to be not only a self-supporting service, but can also be so conducted as to very largely reduce the number and amount of fees which a.re at present charged for the various services performed. There are other matters, but I need hardly dwell on them. I believe that-no matter at what time, remote or near, the larger question of provincial institutions is settled-we require an extension of the powers of this House immediately. Many of them we should have had some time ago. We have been asking for them ever since 1892-asking for them every year.
I have kept the House a great deal longer than I intended and X fear that I have, to some extent, wearied the House. I regret exceedingly that it was not some other hon. gentleman with more ability and more fluency who would have better presented the case and have performed the duty of placing it for the first time before parliament, but, I feel, at all events, that the question is large enough and that the country to which It refers is great enough to create pride in the mind of any one who has the privilege, however poorly, of studying and dealing with it. I trust that when the time comes, whether it comes next year, or the succeeding year, and I feel assured that it will come before the end of the term of this parliament, that parliament may deal with the question on broad principles and endeavour to place the citizens of the Northwest Territories in a position entirely equal, in no way inferior, to the position which is occupied by the citizens of any other province of Canada.
It is not my intention to enter into a discussion of the budget as the ground has been pretty well covered

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Lincoln and Niagara has the floor.
I thought I was next on the list, Mr. Speaker. I put my name down a week ago.
Order, order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Lincoln and Niagara has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, for a long while, or at least, since the 7th November last, I have wondered a good deal how it was that the hon. gentleman who so well represented West Assiniboia in this House for several parliaments was not able to be with us during this parliament, and I am very glad to be able to say that I have discovered the reason. I think I have found it out. Evidently the hon. member who used to be in this House and whom the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott), who has just spoken, succeeded in ousting from that position by obtaining enough votes to enable him to represent that constituency here, must have been defeated at the polls because he was not able to promise to do so many impossible things for the North-west Territories as the hon. gentleman who has succeeded him. I cannot think of anything else that had anything to do with the reversal in the allegiance of that constituency. I have listened to-night with a great deal of attention for an hour and twenty-five minutes to the hon. gentleman who has just sat down, to find out what he had to say about the fiscal policies, about the fiscal policy, if any, of the government, and about the fiscal policy of the opposition. I have listened for over an hour of that time to his discourse on entirely different matters and I give the hon. gentleman a great deal of credit and a great deal of thanks too, because it will serve as an example, as an illustration for me when I shall say a word In regard to the government fiscal policy, which I shall do in a few minutes in the course of my speech. The hon. gentleman who has just sat down has also assisted me by saying that nobody knows to-day, in spite of over a week's debate on the fiscal questions of this country, what is the fiscal policy of the government outside of the members of the cabinet themselves. We have been trying to find that out for four years and we did think, that, although they would not tell the people what their policy was, they would tell the members of parliament when we got into a new parliament after the elections. But, we have not discovered it yet from the members of the cabinet and we find that of those behind the cabinet no two of them agree for one minute as to what that policy is. We have the hon. gentleman who has just sat down discoursing to us; he wants free trade, and he illustrates his position by saying that he does not want a duty on wheat. But he does not say that he would remove the duty on wheat, and he votes for a government that keeps that duty on wheat and votes for a government that does not put a duty on corn. The people of Ontario are more concerned in having a duty on corn than the people of the North-west Territories are in having a
duty on wheat. I know that it is denied that throughout the Dominion there are sectional feelings, I know it is denied that the province of Quebec votes in one way for certain reasons that it ought not to take into consideration, but, while on the floor of this House we find that all the members of the Conservative party stand together as one man on matters of policy, we cannot find hon. gentlemen opposite able to debate the question without bringing in sectional matters that particularly affect their own constituencies. So, if we want an excuse or a justification, for putting on the records of the House a declaration distinctly saying what our policy is, hon. gentlemen opposite have not only given us that excuse, but our regard for the honour of the country forces us to do so because we want to have a policy declared in such a way as to be understood by the ordinary every-day man in this country, so that he can tell his neighbour in Buffalo, or his cousin in Ireland, or England, or Scotland, what kind of laws he is going up against if he emigrates to this country. If we cannot have a policy that every one can understand in that way from the government, the next best thing to do is to have a policy from the opposition, so that if the people will be willing to bide a wee they will know what is going to be the policy of the country when the opposition become the 'government. If we wanted any reason for putting a declaration, or a resolution, upon records of the House such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax), whom I have the honour to follow in this House, has placed upon the records, we have it from the very proceedings, the very arguments which are made by hon. gentlemen opposite in their endeavour to support the government willingly in everything that is done, and everything that the government may do. In 1896-I do not wish to repeat, but it is necessary to make the argument consecutive-it is well known that the government got into power by making certain pledges and it is well known and never disputed that it did not carry out these pledges. In 1900 it was argued upon the hustings of every province-I will not speak specially for the provinces of Quebec, or Manitoba, or for the North-west Territories, because I was not there, and I cannot say what they did there, but it is fair to assume that the same arguments were made there as were made in Ontario, that there was more than one reason why the government should be turned out of office. It was argued that in public matters you could not trust them, and that was given as the reason why they should be turned out. The province of Ontario, which I think, I may say, without wishing to wound the feelings of hon. gentlemen representing other parts of the Dominion, leads the other provinces in civilization and progress, undertook to say by a very large majority that such things as were shown to have been done could not be done in public 64i
life any more than they could be done in private life, that the business of Canada could not be done on that basis, that the affairs of the country must be carried on in a proper and business like way. I have heard many reasons given by hon. gentlemen as to why the government is not better represented on the floor of this House from the province of Ontario ; but, if you look at it in any constituency you like, comparing it with another constituency and applying fair and proper reasoning to it, you will find that the reason which generally actuated the mind of the people, was whether they would or would not employ persons to carry on their business whom they had employed before and who had not carried out what they said they would do. I am not debating now whether free trade or protection is the best policy for the province. I believe protection is the best policy. I have always believed it, I believe it now, and I am caused more than ever to believe it by the fact that some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House admit that it is while all hon. gentlemen on this side of the House say it is. That does not carry a doubt according to the expressions of the cabinet, but it does carry a doubt according to expressions of hon. gentlemen behind and supporting that cabinet. For all these reasons we must conclude that protection is the best policy for this country. But, Sir, the question of whether protection or free trade is the better policy in our interests is not the question that most concerns us as a people. Sir, it is a question of the national honour of Canada ; it is a question as to whether we are to do business in public matters upon the same moral plane as we do business in private matters. I stand here to say that if my hon. leader were to-day to treat the public issues so lightly from a moral standpoint, as have the leaders of the Liberal party I would not come to this parliament to sit behind him and to vote with him on party questions. The hon, gentleman from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) who spoke in favour of protection the other night, was forced before the last elections to issue a special address to his electors in order to make himselif safe and for fear the government would go down, and that he would go down with.it if he did not show to the people that he was' not going to be guided by that sort of political morality-if the word is permissible-which seems to And favour with the Liberals of this country. I say that we are here to-night. Sir, to decide whether the government of this fair Dominion will be obliged to do what it says it will do, or whether it is to be allowed to get into power promising that it will do certain things when in power, and then not only not do them, hut come hack four years afterwards and not pay the ordinary compliment to the people of telling them what they are going to do or what

they are not going to do. This government in effect says to the people of Canada : We told you we would do such and such a thing in order to get to power, hut now that we have power for the second time we will not pay you the compliment to say whether we are free traders or protectionists ; we will let you find that out for yourselves, and we will go as we please on this question so long as we have men behind us to vote to retain us in power. That is the position which the government places the people of Canada in to-day. I say that if we had no better reason to vote for protection and for a business policy such as that propounded by the leader of the opposition there would be sufficient to entitle this amendment to the support of the ordinary individual in the fact that the leader of the opposition has plainly laid down what policy he wants ; has nailed his colours to the mast, and will steer his course towards a plain business policy which every one can understand and rely upon. The gentleman from Annapolis (Mr. Wade) was frank enough to tell us the other night-and these confessions will fall unawares from the lips of gentlemen opposite-that when the Liberals were wandering around in the wilderness of opposition they did this and that and [DOT]the other thing. Well, Sir, I can tell that bon. gentleman that although the Conservative party to-day is in the wilderness of opposition, we will never wander around ; we will always be able to blaze the trees as we go along, so that we can always be found and always find our way back. Today in opposition we place upon record [DOT]what our policy is, and even if it is not a policy that commends itself to every man who may be an utter free trader, it will at least commend itself to every man who has the interests of his people at heart, for he knows where we are going to take him, he knows our record is good, and he knows we never said we would do a thing and refuse to do it afterwards, even though we had made a mistake. Now, Sir, it has been asked me a great many times how it happened that the chief whip of the Liberal party in the last parliament was not returned to this House from a constituency that was supposed to be safe for the Liberals, and how it is that I came here in his stead. I have always thought it better to reserve the explanation as to that until the time arrived when I could state it publicly in the House of Commons. It is due to no qualification of mine, and it is due to no disqualification on the part of Mr. Gibson. The people of the banner electoral district of Lincoln and Niagara, the oldest settled part of Ontario, a place that first had a parliament building in the whole of this Dominion ; a place that first had a lieutenant-governor residing there-and were it not that I see some hon. gentlemen opposite smiling, I would say, a place that is in the forefront of civilization-a district ahead of the rest of the Dominion in age, if age Mr, LANCASTER.
counts for anything ; that electoral district has returned a supporter of the Conservative party to oppose the acts of the Liberal government simply and solely because the electors 'did not know what that government would do if it were returned to power on the 7th of November, for they knew that during its four years of power it had done nothing that it promised to do in the years prior to 1896. That and nothing else caused the constituency of Lincoln and Niagara to send me to this House. And, Sir, although perhaps I should not say so, I trust that my constituents will not find me wanting in representing their interests ; at all events, when I return to them they will never have to accuse me of making false pledges and of promising them something which I did not endeavour to have carried out.
The resolution before us, Sir, has been thoroughly discussed by gentlemen on both sides of the House. It has been explained over and over again by gentlemen on this side of the House, while the gentlemen on the other side do not appear to he able or willing to understand wbat it means. It is pretty well written, it is pretty plain English ; it is protection and it is a preference with Great Britain, that is to say, a mutual preference. My bon. friend from West Assinibola (Mr. Scott), who last spoke, made an able and eloquent argument in favour of the North-west Territories, and I will take the liberty of pointing out to the government what this follower of theirs thinks a man should do in carrying out his duty. That hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) evidently came here determined to see that the Northwest Territories, and his district of West Assiniboia especially, should get full and ample justice at the hands of this parliament.
