For the very same reason Canada can manufacture these articles cheaper. But, the hon. member for East York was going to make another arrangement. He is

strongly in favour of repealing the preferential tariff altogether, or of making it as lie says, more equitable, and I include with him in this position on this question the toon, member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock). These hon. gentlemen say that because of a preferential tariff, as it at present exists, and because of the reduction of 33i per cent on textile fabrics and woollen goods the woollen mills of the country are to be closed up. The hon. member for East York said that for a preferential trade arrangement with Great Britain he was willing to increase the preference to 50 per cent. If the woollen mills cannot stand the present competition, what would become of them it it were increased to 50 per cent ? And I dare say the hon. gentleman would even he willing to add, say 10 or 15 per cent more, in order to strike a bargain ? If the woollen mills are going to be closed up because of the present preference, I suppose they would flourish If it were to be increased to 50 or 60 per cent ? This is the kind of argument that hon. gentlemen opposite address to the House. I was nearly forgetting the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. -Clancy). He appeared to have made a discovery in the remarks that he addressed to the House. He said that the government were taking credit to themselves. because, as a result of giving the preferential tariff to Great Britain, exporters of goods to this country, similar to those manufactured in Great Britain, were obliged to bring the price down to the amount of the preference and he entirely controverted that position. He said that it would never operate in that way at all.*' Am I right in making that statement ?

The hon. gentleman asks if he is right in making the statement that I entirely controverted it. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman.
He has figured it out to his owu satisfaction that the preference to Great Britain only amounts to thirty-five one hundredths of one per cent, but he and his friends say in the same breath that the Prime Minister went to England and gave away valuable concessions and got absolutely nothing in return. I leave it to gentlemen opposite to settle these inconsistencies and contradictions among themselves. I again come back to the statement made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) that the preference the present government gives Great Britain does not reduce the price of similar articles coming into this country from other countries, while on the other hand he tells us that if Great Britain put a duty upon corn and wool and meat and other products going into her markets and gave Canada a preference, then every other country sending similar articles into Great Britain would have to come down to the extent of the preference.

That was not it.
Mr. HUGHES (P.E.I.) Oh, yes, that was it.

I endeavoured to point out that the class of goods imported from other countries to this country were of a different kind, although they may be classified the same, and therefore could not come into competition; and that other countries had separate fields from Great Britain. There are two distinct fields, as the hon. gentleman knows, and therefore they cannot come into competition.
Mr. HUGHES (P.E.I.) The remarks of the hon. gentleman are on record and any person can read them. He may wish to make an explanation now, hut we all know what he said the other evening. Some hon. gentlemen opposite have asked what the present administration have done.

Then, I am stating the case correctly as far as he is concerned. A little later on he said that if we had a preference with England and England would put a duty on corn, meat and other products coining from Canada it would not increase the price of these articles because all other countries exporting similar articles to Britain would have to come down in the price equal to the preference to Canada. It would appear, therefore, that the laws of trade and commerce would work one way in Canada, and in directly an opposite way in Great Britain.

The hon. gentleman quite misunderstood me. It has been pointed out that we send a mere fraction, and must always send a mere fraction of the bread-stuffs to England, and therefore the greater must bear the burden instead of the smaller. That is the distinction.
Mr. HUGHES (P.E.I.) The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) is very strong in fractions.

I never asked that.
Mr. HUGHES (P.E.I.) Well, I can tell the hon. gentleman that this government since it came into power have made very great improvements and developments in the Post Office Department; they have reorganized and rejuvenated the militia of this country; they have extended the Intercolonial Railway into Montreal, and, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) said the other day, they have turned a dead railway into a live one; they have provided cold storage and transportation facilities so that the immense exports of products from this country have become possible; they have provided such facilities that the fruit and other perishable products of Canada at the Paris exposition were able to carry off the lion's share of the prizes in competition with the whole world. This government have done a great many other things since they have been in power, and I belfeve they have fully satisfied the

people of Canada. I suppose tliey do not claim that they possess all the wisdom of the earth. They are not infallible or impeccable, but they are at least an earnest, honest, patriotic, progressive body of men who are giving their time and the best of wliat is in them for the true development of our country, and the people of Canada appreciate it. Well, Sir, some of these gentlemen opposite have been rehearsing- their campaign speeches, and we were told'by the hon. member from Wentworth (Mr. Smith) and the hon. member from West York (Mr. Wallace) and others, that the miserable and disreputable race cry that was started in the province of Quebec last year, had some considerable influence upon the elections. I do not know what influence the race cry may lnive had, but 1 want to say that that miserable and disreputable race cry was started in a very small corner of the province of Quebec, namely in the Star newspaper office in Montreal. Perhaps it had no influence in the province of Ontario, I hope it had none, but hon. gentlemen opposite are the best judges of the effect which the race and religious cry was expressly intended to have there. Now, Sir, as to the amendment before the House. In the words of an eminent authority, the language is delightfully vague. It says :
That, in the opinion of this House, the welfare of this country reqiures a pronounced policy of adequate protection and encouragement at all times to the labour, agricultural, manufacturing, mining and other industrial interests of Canada.
That, in the opinion of this House, the adoption of a policy of mutual trade preference within the empire would prove of great benefit to the mother country and to the colonies, and would greatly promote the prosperity, unity and progress of the empire as a whole, and that the present time, when the Commonwealth of Australia is laying the foundation of its fiscal system, is particularly opportune for taking prompt and energetic steps towards the furtherance of this object.
So there is to be high protection for the manufacturers, free trade for the farmers; riches for everybody, everything you want and if there is anything you want and do not see all you have to do Is to ask for It.
This House is further of opinion that equivalent or adequate duties should be imposed by Canada upon the products and manufactures of countries not within the empire in all cases where such countries fail to admit Canadian products and manufactures upon fair terms, and that the government should take for this purpose all such available measures as may be found necessary.
When the leader of the opposition was speaking to this part of the resolution, he declared that he would not approve of bringing it into effect against the United States and, of course, it does not apply to Great Britain, or any paid: of the empire. Therefore, as 87 per cent of our whole trade is with Great Britain and the United States, this part of the resolution would be prac-Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.)
tically a dead letter. It would appear as if the resolution has been so worded that hon, gentlemen opposite can go throughout the country and take whatever meaning they like out of it. It is the hope of these hon. gentlemen that all those who are in distress and oppressed with difficulty, and under any affliction of mind may gather around the leader of the opposition and that he may become their prince in the cave of Adullam, and in this way he may perhaps gather around him a party sufficiently strong to some time in the distant future return him to power. For the reasons I have given, Mr. Speaker, and for many many others, I am a supporter of the present administration. I am both an old Liberal and a new Liberal, because I do not think there is any difference between the two. The hon. member from Toronto (Mr. Brock) told us that the Conservatives were not ashamed of anything in their past history. He is a very fortunate man indeed who has no skeleton in the family cupboard. I do not think that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) has been a close reader of political events in the years 1891 and 1873 and 1849, or else he would know, that if all the skeletons in the political cupboards of the Conservative party were revealed, they would astonish even the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock). For the reasons I have given I am a supporter of the Liberal party, and I shall be obliged to vote against the amendment. I thank you. Mr. Speaker, and hon. members for their patient hearing.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose, at this stage of the debate, to go into the figures connected with the budget. They have been elaborately dealt with by members on both sides of the House. I wish merely to confine myself to a few observations which have occurred to me as I listened to the debate, which I followed most patiently and carefully. The most striking feature of the debate, so far as I have been able to see, has been the declaration on the part of a number of Liberals, that while they are free traders in theory, they are still'willing to support protection in practice. I must say that I have listened with regret to many declarations on the part of Liberals that they are willing to accept a protective tariff.
Now, it seems to me that if there is one thing which is desirable in this country at the present time, it is that we should get down to clear definitions. I think it is particularly desirable that we should have a distinct and authoritative statement as to whether the tariff which we have is a protective tariff or a tariff for revenue only. I think. Sir-and I am sure that you and lion, members will agree with me-that it is not a good thing, either in the interest of the country or in our own interest, that we should either practice any deception on the
country or allow any deception to be practised on ourselves. Either this tariff is a protective tariff or it is a tariff for revenue only. My own conviction is that the tariff has not been scaled down to the point of a revenue tariff. I may say that this tariff question was discussed very elaborately in my constituency during an exciting campaign which was waged there previous to the election. Some speakers contended that the tariff had been scaled down to a revenue basis, and that the government, in revising the tariff in 1897, had wiped out entirely the element of protection. The position I took at that time was this. I gave to my audiences three statements with regard to the tariff. I quoted the statement which was frequently made by the Hon. Geo. E. Foster, who, as you know, was the financial critic of the opposition during the last parliament, that the total reduction in the tariff made by this government amounted to 71-100ths of 1 per cent. I merely gave his statement for what it was worth. Mr. *Joseph Martin, a Liberal of rugged independence, a very prominent figure in this country, and one who occupied a prominent position in this House, made the statement at a public meeting in Winnipeg some years ago, that the reductions in the tariff amounted to less than 1 per cent. I gave that statement for what it was worth. Then, I remember listening to a speech which my hon. friend the present Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) made in the city of Winnipeg a little over a year ago, in which he made the claim, if my memory serves me correctly-and he will correct me if I do not present the actual fact-that the reduction had been 21 per cent on the tariff, or 10 per cent if you bring it to cash. Therefore, I said there were three statements with regard to the tariff-the first by a Conservative, the second by a Liberal, and the third by a member of this government. Now, I put the matter in this way-and I think hon. members will agree that it was perfectly fair ; I think the country at least expected, from the ante-election pledges of the Liberal party, and from the Ottawa platform, that if we did not get free trade as they have it in England, which my right hon. friend the leader of the government declared to be his own ideal, we would, at , any rate, get a tariff for revenue only. The question then arose, what is a tariff for revenue only ? Under the administration of the late Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, we had what I think the country regarded as a tariff for revenue only. That tariff, as you know, was a 174 per cent tariff. In 1878 when the Liberal government of the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie was defeated and the Conservatives came into power, they inaugurated what was known as the national policy, and imposed a tariff which has generally been regarded as averaging 35 per cent. If we were to get a purely revenue
tariff, I think the popular expectation' was that we should get a 171 per cent tariff. Instead of that, if you accept the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Customs -and we will take his statement, and disregard those of Mr. Foster and Mr. Martin -we have a tariff of 324 per cent.
Therefore, what the country and this House have to consider is this : Is a reduction of 2J per cent a wiping out of the element of protection from the tariff ? Now,
I may frankly say that I do not consider that it is ; and, as I said at the outset, I believe if there is one thing desirable in the country at the present time, it is perfect frankness in regard to this matter. Either we have a revenue tariff or we have a protective tariff. I have never been disposed to be hypercritical of the government with regard to the reduction of the tariff. We had conditions established in the country extending over a priod of twenty years; we had industries in full operation, which had grown up under the protective tariff, and it was not reasonable to expect the government to wipe out the tariff, or even to cut it down at one swoop to 171 per cent which was Mackenzie's revenue tariff. Therefore, I was never disposed to he hypercritical of the policy the government adopted ; and when the Finance Minister, in 1897, at the time the revision was made, warned the manufacturers that eternal vigilance would be the price of protection, and when he gave the country clearly to understand that there would be a general scaling down of the customs duties from time to time, I may say that as a western man I was disposed to accept that. I was disappointed, however, when the tariff was announced, for we had reason to expect mat the duties would have been taken off agricultural implements and coal oil, and other necessities of the farmers. But, the country was in a very kindly mood, and was very generously disposed towards the government, and, as the people felt that there would be a scaling down of the duties from time to time, as intimated by the Minister of Finance, they were disposed to be satisfied. Even in the west, where the disappointment with regard to the tariff was very severe, the people were disposed to treat the government with the utmost generosity.
But what is the position now ? I remember very well my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, in that speech to which I have referred, turning to the vast audience in the city of Winnipeg and drawing their attention to the reduction of 2i per cent and asking them if they wex-e not now satisfied. Let me recall also the statement made by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) in his speech at Perth, in which he said, that the tariff was a settled question and had been taken out of the list of issues in this country. And, during my campaign, I was able to quote a statement

made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Parte) at a. banquet in Valleyfield, where he assured the cotton kings that the tariff would not be interfered with. Therefore we may reasonably conclude that the settled policy of this government seems to be stability of tariff.
This session we hoped to 'have the duty on coal oil wiped out. That was one of the great issues during the last four or five years when the Liberal party was in opposition. That duty was' made to do service on every Liberal platform from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and the people of the Northwest had reason to expect that this very high duty would be removed.
Prom what I could learn, I feared that this session the former duty on lumber would have been reimposed, and X. listened with great regret to the remarks of the bon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) on that point. If there is one thing in the North-west which we need it Is lumber. There are no pine forests in that country, and we have to get our lumber from, Ontario or Minnesota, and if the duty were reimposed it would inflict great hardship on our people, who require a great deal of lumber in building granaries and stables and sheds to protect their cattle and horses in the very severe weather.
As far as I can judge, we are more likely to have the tariff raised than lowered, and if such he the case, I would like to sound a warning note to the Liberals of this country. I think it is fair to assume that, owing to the educative campaign which was conducted for twenty years prior to iSP6, at -least one-half of our people have been converted to the idea of free trade or at least a tariff for revenue only. But, we have to-day the spectacle of the Liberal party being gradually led -along the path of high duties with a prospect of being ultimately delivered right into the fold of protection, body and boots. If that be the case, a warning note ought to be sounded. I believe that the great mass of the Liberal party in this country is sound on this tariff question. I do not believe that the people want protection, and it seems to me that official Liberalism stands in this position : The voice is the voice of free trade Jacob, but the hands are the hands of protective Esau.
I like to toe perfectly frank. I think it is desirable that we should call a spade a spade, and if our present policy tariff be a protective tariff-and I believe it is-and if a protective tariff was toad for twenty years before 1896, it is equally toad at present. So far as I aim concerned, representing a large constituency in the west, I hope that I will he given grace to raise my voice from time to time against the protective tariff. Exotic industries not indigenous to the country at all are protected by huge bounties. But the farmer is protected in no way whatever. The question of the duty on wheat

was brought up to-night. One hon. member wanted to know if the hon. member for West Assinlboia (Mr. Scott) was willing to agree to the abrogation of the duty on wheat. Well, as far a-s I am concerned, I would be perfectly satisfied to have the duty -taken off wheat altogether, and I believe so would the farmers of the west. The Ministers of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and Customs (Mr. Paterson) will recall that when they conducted an inquiry with regard to the operation of the tariff, in the council chamber at Winnipeg, -a large deputation of farmers from all over the province appeared before them and declared in favour of taking off the duty on wheat. The people of the west do not desire protection. but if you are going to protect these industries in the east-the iron and coal industries-toy giving thorn bounties, I would like to put in a plea for a bounty to the farmers of the North-west on -growing their wheat.
The future of Canada lies in its vast plains to the west, and unless you make the conditions of that country such that the settlers will he able to procure their necessaries cheaply, you are not going to promote the success of that country as you should.
I am no prophet, but I think those hon. gentlemen who have traversed our western plains, will agree with me that in probably a decade, the balance of power in Canada will be vested in- that country. I remember well when the right hon. leader of the government was wont to make strong pleas in behalf of that country. I am disposed to believe that his heart still beats in sympathy with the people of the North-west, and I would appeal to him to-night not to allow the protective idea to prevail in our tariff.
Something is due to the North-west, if we desire -that country to succeed as it should. And in that connection I would urge a plea against the introduction of too many European immigrants into that country. We have on the plains sufficient now of these foreign immigrants. Land is becoming scarce, such as we have in Manitoba. and we -can well afford to hold these fertile plains for our own sons. Let us put there the best classes of people we can procure, people with broad ideas, people with good blood, people in whom we have confidence. Let us settle these people on the plains, and then we will have a population that will assist instead of retard us in our progress, a population which will be able to exercise intelligence in the politics of -this 'Country and work along the right lines when the time comes for them to receive the franchise.
Now, although not strictly germane to -this question in view of the great latitude that has been allowed in this debate, I would like to say this-that I think it would be desirable to have the government enunciate a clear policy with regard to railway bonus-ing, the construction of railways and the ex-
[DOT]2045

tension of our canals. Take, for instance, | tlie Trent Valley canal, into which, I think, some seven or eight millions of the country's money has been poured In past years. Let me remind my Liberal friends in this House that for all these years they contended against that expenditure as one utterly use-1 less, and now we are going on pouring further millions into that enterprise. I think that is a mistake. We have now expended on our canal system some eighty millions of dollars; and thoughtful men who have studied the question of transportation in this country, I think, will agree that that money has, to a very large extent, been wasted. I do not think that our canal sys-tern has been satisfactory; I do not think there are any set of men in this country today who have a clear and intelligent view as to what the aim should be with regard to the canal system. I would appeal to the House, that, before spending more money, a definite scheme should be formulated so that at least we may cease to expend millions uselessly on the canals. As to the question of railway bonusing, I think that public opinion in this country is growing so strong, that in recent months if not in recent years feeling against this system has so increased that the people will not justify the giving of one dollar further of bonuses to any railway company, more especially in the settled districts of Canada. I think we should allow it to be understood that Canada has reached the stage when a franchise to construct a road is valuable even without a bonus. I do not think we should go further in paying for the railroads of this country and handing them over to exploiters to tax us heavily under the head of freight rates.
I would like to say one word with regard to the public expenditures of Canada. I may be accused of being a cheese-parer, but I am quite willing to be so classed. There was not a declaration of the Liberal party in which I more heartily acquiesced than that made by the Hon. Mr. Mills and endorsed by the hon. premier and also by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies). If you put us in power, said these hon. gentlemen prior to 1896, we will be able to reduce the amount charged for running the machine by two or three-and I think they went as far as to say four or five-millions of dollars. I think they were perfectly sincere in that. In discussing this question with a Liberal friend the other day, he said: 'Mr. Richardson, I do not think this country wants any reform, I do not think the people desire It; what they want is a liberal expenditure of money, and, for my part I have come to the conclusion that it is scarcely worth while trying to advocate any reform in this country.' If that proposition is true, it is an appaling one, and one that every member should take into serious consideration. It may be that our
friends who sit on the treasury benches have come to the conclusion that they would not make the mistakes that Mackenzie made-if they were mistakes-and that the country desires a lavish expenditure of money. If they have conscientiously reached that conclusion, I think it is most unfortunate. I believe that we can save not merely three or four or five millions in the public expenditure, but possibly seven or eight millions. I believe that the departments are loaded up far beyond the necessities of the public service, and I believe that all along the line great savings could be effected. I believe, further, that in this time of prosperity, when Providence has smiled upon us- (I do not attribute good times to the action of the government, though I would not like to deprive the government of any credit due to them in facilitating the matter so far as in them lies)-now that we are having these years of plenty, we ought to take serious stock of our affairs and endeavour, as far as possible, to curtail the public expenditure and reduce the public debt. I believe the time will come, and come soon, when we shall not have as good times as we have now, and instead of large surpluses- on the possession of which I congratuate the country-we will have to face deficits. And it is well, in view of these possibilities, that we should exercise great economy in running our affairs. I believe with ex-President Cleveland that public office Is a public trust. To my mind no statesman or philosopher ever made a better declaration than that. Without lecturing the House, I think we should get our minds fairly seized of that idea. And if the members of the government were fairly seized of that idea, I believe greater care would be exercised with regard to the distribution of bonuses and with regard to expenditures generally. I believe that the distribution of these bonuses is one of the causes, perhaps the principal cause, of the corruption that prevails throughout the country at the present day. I am not prepared to say that corruption is especially due to the operations of the Liberals or operations of the Conservatives ; both parties are to my mind equally blameworthy. All men who are fair-minded know that corruption exists to a very large extent at the present time. I think it would be the duty of public men to put an effective veto on corruption. I do not see anything higher they could do in the interest of humanity than that corruption should be wiped out as far as possible.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Where is it ?

If the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Ross) does not know that there is corruption in this country, it would be quite useless for me to attempt to enlighten him. I say that, inasmuch an

these bonuses are the greatest sources, in my estimation, of corruption, I believe that the sooner we stop them and the sooner the government secures control of the railways and of transportation, the better it will be in the best interests of the country. For, after all, the loss of a few hundreds of thousands of dollars, in my opinion, is nothing compared with the demoralization of the people.
Now, I am sure lion, gentlemen will realize, in view of the statements that I have made, that it will be impossible for me to support the amendment. The amendment calls for adequate protection to our industries. I think our so-called industries have been protected entirely too much, and the period of protection has been already too long. I believe the time has come not merely for lopping away the mouldering branches, hut for stripping the tree comparatively bare. I believe that most of these industries should stand upon their own feet without protection, and, believing so, I find it impossible to support the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition. I am not here to say that I think free trade is possible in Canada at the present. I believe, that for a long time to come at least, it will be necessary to raise our revenue by tariff duties.
My hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) made to-night what I think was a very convincing argument, when he quoted the figures of the revenue received under the 85 per cent protective tariff on agricultural implements which prevailed prior to 1894, and the figures of the revenue received under the tariff revised by the Conservative party in 1894, that is, when the duties were reduced on agricultural implements from 35 per cent to 20 per cent. My hon. friend was able to show that the revenue increased five or ten times, I think ; anyway, to an enormous extent. I was going to suggest to him that he would have made his argument even stronger had he taken the year 1899 instead of 1900. He shakes his head, probably he knows, having gone over the figures. The reason why I think the argument would have been stronger if taken from 1899 is, that last year, as hon. gentlemen know, we had a very serious crop failure in Manitoba, and there was a much smaller purchase of agricultural implements for that reason. I believe that had he taken 1899 he would have been able to make a better comparison. However, his comparison was sufficient to satisfy me and to satisfy all hon. members in this House that you can gather more revenue out of a lower tariff than from a high one; that you make nothing out of a protective tariff, you simply put money into the pockets of the manufacturers instead of into the public exchequer. This argument reminded me of the language I used to hear from the leader of the House in the Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
old days, and which appealed to me especially as a young man, who was sitting at the feet of Gamaliel and receiving lessons with regard to protection and free trade. I may say that so far as my own view goes, I stand by the position which I have held for the last fifteen or twenty years with regard to the tariff. As a western man I do not see how I could take any other position, because if there is one thing that the country requires, it is to have the duties lowered or wiped out altogether from the necessaries of the settlers.

Mr. Speaker, I shall have to speak this evening to a very thin House, as I see that a good many members are absent. Now, Sir, I think it would be well, if we really are the servants of the people, that our masters should send spotters to this House to see how their servants are attending to their duties, because I notice many seats on both sides of the House are empty. I think that is not what we get our indemnity for. I do not wish to be critical, I do not wish to be hard on the members that are absent, because they cannot hear me. I have sat here since this House opened, and I have noticed a great many times that the ministerial benches were occupied either by the Prime Minister or the Finance Minister ; one of them is always in his seat, more often the Prime Minister. Now, if I have said anything that will induce a member to be in his seat regularly, I think I have accomplished something. As regards the question before the House, I do not suppose I can throw much light upon it. I must say, however, after listening to the discussion from both sides of the House, that it has turned more often on something else than either the budget or the amendment. The question has been discussed at great length from the political standpoint, and I think the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) is the only member that has spoken this evening from the Independent standpoint. I think it is my duty to take the same line. I was, as you know, elected an independent, and I intend to pursue that course as long as I sit in this House. I will support any government as long as they bring down good measures ; as long as they are truthful, faithful and honest to this country I will support them.
Now, this question of the budget is a very difficult thing, perhaps, for a farmer to undertake to criticise. But if I criticise it at all it will be from the farmer's standpoint. You know that politics run very high in this country, they say there is more politics in Canada to the square inch than in any other country in the world, and I believe it. I was at a threshing bee some years ago, and I am going to tell you what I heard. I see it is in order to tell stories in this House, to talk religion, to do almost anything, so I will tell you a story showing
the condition of politics in the section of country in which 1 live. Two farmers, both ol' them intelligent men, were discussing politics-there were over a dozen of us present. The two men grew quite warm over it, very warm indeed, and one of them broke out in language something like
this : ' The Tories may all go to 

' he
meant Hades, but he said another place- into the place where his Satanic majesty resides, 1 believe. The other gentleman replied : ' There is one thing certain, there will be no Grits in heaven.' I came to the conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that I would remain an Independent, because heaven was not made in vain, and the Independents will be there sure.
Now, there are a number of things in the budget that I think are all right. There are some things, perhaps, in the amendment that may be all right; but I have been a free trader for over fifty years, and 1 cannot swallow the high protective duty in that amendment. I say this much, as I admire many of the actions of the hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, for I believe they are in earnest, I believe they are trying to do as their constituents told them to do ; but when they advocate a high protective tariff, which means that the farmers of this country will have to pay higher for everything that they require, and probably get less for everything they raise, then I am sure I cannot possibly follow them. Then, they say that they are opposed to the preferential tariff with Great Britain. On that question I have my ideas. I stop and think of what happened in years gone by. I always thought that the Conservative party were the most loyal party we had. I thought they were true, and especially true to the mother country, but when I find that they stand out so strongly against the preferential tariff, I exclaim : ' Oh, how my idol is shattered.'
I am sorry for one reason that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Bichard Cartwright) is not in his seat. He is getting old now like myself and it requires an active, smart, able, young man to fill that position because he has to look out markets for us. I am sorry, and I think he is sorry too, that he made a speech five years ago when he said that the office which he now holds, and to which he was about to be promoted, was of no use whatever, in fact, that it was like the fifth wheel to the coach. Further, he said, that if we raised more than $38,000,000 it would be a disgrace and a shame. I am reminded that the Psalmist said : ' Oh. that mine enemy would write a book.' The hon. gentleman's political foes say, ' Oh, that mine enemy would make a speech.' because it comes back on him and tells with great force against him. As far as the budget is concerned, it is a very difficult matter. If the Independents of this House were in power we would find it perhaps very diffi-65
cult to arrange so that we could make both ends meet or come out within half a million of dollars of doing so. We would perhaps have as much difficulty as the members of the government have. However, we would bo in hopes that we would have the balance on the right side of the ledger and have something more instead of having a deficit. We would rather have a favourable balance, but, we believe that it is the duty of the government to raise as much as they require to meet the expenditure of the country and that when they raise more money which is not required it seems to me that they should do what every good farmer would do, who had a mortgage on his farm. He would not go and spend the money on finery or on furniture. He would pay off the mortgage, but, instead of that we find that the government, in the last four or five years have added about $7,000,000 to the public debt. It seems to me that the government should at least live within their income and pay off something of the national debt. That is what I believe should be done with the surplus. However, they have thought otherwise. As far as this question of trade is concerned, I may say that those hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who are asking for increased protection, who advocate high duties on everything that is manufactured in this country, and who propose to prevent British goods coming in here in order to protect people who are engaged in business, take a position with which I do not agree. Of course, we do not blame hon. members who represent urban constituencies and are endeavouring to please their constituents, but, on the other hand, those of us who represent rural constituencies will not be justified in going back to their constituents and telling them that they have advocated a high protective tariff. I do not see how they can square themselves with their constituents. What does a high protective tariff mean ? It means that some few men are going to become immensely rich while the rest of us are immensely poor. If you cannot get a sufficient number of specimens of this class of people in our own country you only have to cross the border and you will find millionaires and multi-millionaires whose wealth is the result of protection. Carnegie does not know what to do with his money. He is bringing some of it to Ottawa. He does not know what to do with the money he has made out of the farmers and out of the fools in the United States. There are hundreds of men like him and it is all brought about by high protection in that country. We have been following here in the same footsteps. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House want to continue in his footsteps.
Hear, hear.

An hon. gentleman says ' hear, hear.' Well, he is not a farmer ; he does not have to pay for it. Now, wo are told that this government had



the largest surplus that was ever produced in Canada. According to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), this is not the largest, and I have not heard his statement contradicted. I was expecting to hear it contradicted on the other side of the House. The hon. member for Pictou most emphatically says that there have been greater sur-. pluses under some other governments than under the present government. However,
I will leave that for you to settle amongst yourselves. I am quite content that the government should hare a deficit in the post office. If the government have acted in any one way that is beneficial to this country it is the way In which the post office has been conducted. They have reduced the postage in Canada, and we all know how cheap postage encourages trade. I am satisfied the government are justified in doing it. As far as sending soldiers to South Africa is concerned, I am sure the country will endorse the expenditure of public money for that service. It has given us an advertisement and has shown to Great Britain where the hearts of Canadians lie. In regard to the tariff it was expected, and I was expecting it myself, that when this government came into power they would surely carry out the pledges they had given to us. and I would tell hon. gentlemen on this side of the House that if you were tomorrow to change places, it is quite possible that you may not be able to carry out aU the things you are saying in opposition. I notice that I have the attention of the House and I thank hon. gentlemen very much for it. I am afraid I am wearying you.
Go on.

I was in hopes that the government would carry out their free trade policy, but it seems that they found it almost impossible to do so. I have no doubt that they did the very best they could. But, if they do not carry out their policy and if they continue in the course of extravagance in expenditure and in the appointing of unnecessary officials, they will be sure to hear from somebody on this side of the House. Why, Sir, I have heard, and it is more than hearsay, that when the Conservatives were on the Treasury benches for eighteen years they appointed seventeen supporters of theirs from this House to offices of emolument.
Hear, hear.

You gentlemen over there laugh about that, but I find from the record that the present government have only been five years in power and they have appointed twelve of their friends from the House of Commons to office, so they went the Tories one better. It is a shame for any honourable man who is elected to serve for five years in this parliament to go begging and sneaking around Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
the ministers to ask an office. It is a worse disgrace for the members than for the government which appoints them. Now, Mr. Speaker, I hope that will not occur again.
Hear, hear.

I do not pose as a critic generally, but I say what I think and I am not ashamed of it, and I am not afraid to meet any man, and you need not be if you do what is right. I just thought that this government when they promised so many things would have at least given to the farmers free coal oil. Coal oil is the farmers' electric light and the farmers' gas. He takes it in the morning to the barn to do his chores, and at night he burns it in his household. The mechanic, the labouring man, and the farmer use it, but the people of the cities care little about the price of coal oil, because they do not burn it. Now, five cents a gallon makes quite a big item to the farmer and we thought that this government would leave Mr. Rockefeller on one side and that we ' fellers' would get some help, but instead of that Rockefeller got it. I suppose there was some influence brought to bear upon the government, and that the monopolists were taken care of while the farmers got left. We thought that agricultural implements would be allowed in free, and although they were reduced to 20 per cent, still 20 per cent is quite a good deal from the farmers' point of view.
Who reduced that duty ?

Not you. I hope you gentlemen will not catechise me because you put me out, and when I get done, you can speak as long and as fast as you like, but let me have a chance now. The average life of a binder is ten years. The first binder I purchased cost me $200, and the next $120. Capitalize the interest and see how much it costs a farmer for bis binders. Now if this money went into the treasury of the country it would not be so bad, but it goes into the pockets of men who form trusts and put up the price of binders on the farmers, and the government gets no revenue. Consequently the government should take some action in this matter especially for the benefit of these poor people who live on the prairies.
Hear, hear.
You think I am making a point in your favour, but just wait a little until I get at you. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is nearly twelve o'clock and I must conclude.
Go on.

I am the only man in this House except the Prime

Minister that you gentlemen tell to go on and speak. When I came down here one gentleman said to me : You will have a very short session this time because all the long-winded fellows are left at home, but I find that we have got some long-winded men left, and all you have to do is to wind them up and they will go on as long as you like, and say very little when they have done. Now, Sir, I do not intend to give the government much advice. I am not going to wield the patronage in my county, and I would not if I had the privilege of doing it. Anyway, the government would not listen to me if I did give them advice, but if they expect to get the votes of the farmers of this country they have got to do as they promised to do. Let them, carry out their pledges. The government, of course, are only men like the rest of us and they are subject to influence if the right influence Is brought to bear upon them. When a man says he is above temptation I begin to think that he has not had sufficient offered to him. Perhaps the reason that I am honest is that 1 have not been tempted, and I do not expect that the government is going to tempt me. Now, Sir, while I have been sitting here for the last eight or nine days listening to this debate I have taken enough notes to fill half a bushel measure, but I cannot use them to-night, and as the budget will not be discussed again I think I had better keep them until next year's budget. There are several things here I would like to speak about. I am strongly opposed to the members of the government taking part in the elections, and you know that in the old country they do not allow a man who has a title to go on the stump and advise the people as to how they should vote. I should like to see the titled gentlemen in this country adopt that system, and if they did the people would have a great deal more respect for them. I noticed that all last week two of the ministers were missing, and it was quite a while before I found out where they were. I discovered at last that there were some public works to be erected away up in North Bruce, and of course they had to be looked after. Again, I found that the hon. member for West Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. Hackett) had a grievance, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries Hon. Sir Louis Davies) went down to look after that. I do not think that kind of thing is right. Just before the election in East Elgin the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was up there, and I am sorry he is not in his place because I do not like to say a word behind a man's back that I would not say before his face. The Minister of Public Works came up into our county with his jaunting car or some other car, and what for ? Well, to build a drill shed. Along about the 5th November he set to dig a hole in the ground and turned the sod with a silver shovel, and that kind of thing and the people became disgusted. Gentle-654
men, if you want to know why you lost East Elgin do not ask any more questions. It is too thin ; a great deal too thin ; it does not do. In the constituency I represent we have not got a five-cent piece of government money invested except it be a railway which last year you built parallel to another line and to which you gave $3,200 a mile. Unless you count that, I do not think my constituency has got a five-cent piece which the government have put into it. So we do not owe them anything ; and my constituents did not send them a supporter on that account, but they sent a man.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to detain the House any further; it is within ten minutes of midnight. I know that the rules of the House do not permit me to move an adjournment; but I will give you my sentiments on this question :
That in the opinion of this House close trade relations between all the British colonies and the mother country would be the means of strengthening the empire, and that some system of fair trade, leading to freer trade, should be inaugurated ; that, in the meantime, all the infant industries of this country should be assisted until they are able to stand alone, but not after ; that all raw material used in manufactures shall be admitted free, as far as practicable- and I mean to include in that binders, which are part of the farmer's raw material ; that the revenue required for the expenditure of the country shall be raised on the luxuries of life as far as possible ; that 50 per cent instead of 33J per cent be taken off the duties on all kinds of British goods ; and that a reciprocal duty be placed against all other countries whenever it is not prejudicial to the best interests of this country.
Now, this is something of my own getting up ; I did not consult anybody as to this. But if I had an opportunity of moving an amendment, that is iwhat I would move.
I do not know that I should say any more, except to give you an illustration of what I mean by infant industries. There was a great big strapping boy, who had grown to be quite a big lad, and who had learned to swear before he was weaned. His mother had not weaned him for several reasons-I will not give them. His mother had company call one day. It was tony company, and she took them into the parlor. The boy was out playing in the mud and dirt, and he ran into the house where the mother was, and cried : ' Mother, I want some tit.' Mother said : ' Go away, you naughty boy ; what do you mean ?' He had learned to say bad words ; I suppose he had been playing with some Grit boys ; and he went in again more ferocious than before, and shouted : ' Mother, I must have some tit.' She said : ' You little dog, go away.' He persisted, and went in again and cried out to the mother : and that night he got such a spanking that he was weaned, and

[DOT]2056
never wanted any more ' tit.' So these infant industries are strong in comparison, but still they want * tit.' Now, Mr. Speaker, I think it is time to close these remarks.
May I ask the right hon. leader of the government if he will agree to the adjournment of the debate ? If so, I move that the debate be adjourned.

There has been, I understand, a private agreement for the closing of the debate. For my part, I am quite willing to agree to the motion of njy hon. friend, but, I suppose, considering the number of gentlemen who want to speak, that it will not be possible to close the debate to-morrow.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: I would have preferred, as far as I am personally concerned, that the debate should be closed to-morrow. If, however, it is the sense of the House that that cannot be done, of course I shall only have to submit. But, I think it is very desirable that it should be closed to-morrow, if it is at all possible.
I do not think it will be possible. It would be better to understand that it will close on Thursday.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
On motion of the Prime Minister, House adjourned at midnight.
Tuesday, March 26, 1901.
